findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async fetch_plan_limits stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine but its only I/O is `requests.get(...)`, a synchronous call. Awaiting this coroutine from the event loop blocks every other task on that loop until the HTTP call returns — up to the full 5 second timeout, and longer if DNS/connect hangs before the timeout applies. Under request handling this serialises all concurrent requests served by that worker.

The module already has the correct shape one function above: `fetch_plan` takes an `httpx.AsyncClient` and does `await client.get(...)`. Either follow that pattern (accept an `AsyncClient` and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`), or, if the synchronous client must stay, offload it with `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, ...)`. The `import requests` on line 2 can then be dropped.

No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this function never worked correctly, returned malformed data, or blocked the event loop. Since the PR's stated purpose is to add this plan-limits fetch for the UI, at minimum a test exercising fetch_plan_limits's return value (e.g. mocking the HTTP call) is warranted to catch behavioral regressions.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. Nothing in this function validates `tenant_id` or percent-encodes it before it becomes part of the path. If the value originates from a request parameter, a caller can supply segments such as `../admin` or `..%2f..%2f` to reach endpoints on `billing.internal` other than `/limits/`, or append `?`/`#` to inject query state — reaching an internal service that is presumably not otherwise exposed to external callers.

Fix by validating the identifier against an expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before use, or by passing it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. Better still, pass it as a parameter the HTTP client escapes for you rather than concatenating into the path.

Note the same pattern exists on line 6 for the pre-existing `fetch_plan`, so a shared validation helper would cover both.

Callers expecting an awaitable that performs async I/O will block the event loop. Either rename to `get_plan_limits` to signal it is blocking, or rewrite to use the async client that `fetch_plan()` already depends on.

findings.title: Bare `except` swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, which includes `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `asyncio.CancelledError`. A Ctrl-C or a cancelled task that lands inside `_client.send` will be silently converted into a successful-looking `return None`, breaking shutdown and cancellation semantics.

The PR description says "catch and log", but there is no logging in the handler, so every push failure — including genuine bugs such as a `TypeError` from a malformed payload — disappears without trace. Narrow the clause to the exception type the client raises (or at minimum `Exception`) and emit a log record with the exception, e.g. `except Exception: logger.exception("metrics push failed")`.

findings.title: Rate limit bypassable: unsynchronised check-then-act in try_consume
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 — all outside `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` (line 9) correctly holds for the same state.

Two consequences, both attacker-reachable by simply issuing requests concurrently (the normal mode of an async server):

1. **Limit bypass.** N coroutines can each pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check on line 16 before any of them writes, so N*cost is admitted against a budget of `cost`. The amount over the limit scales with the attacker's concurrency.
2. **Lost updates make the bypass permanent.** Line 19 assigns an absolute value computed from a stale read rather than incrementing, so concurrent calls clobber each other's accounting. The stored counter drifts permanently below actual consumption, meaning the limiter never catches up even after the burst ends.

Fix: hold the lock across the read, the decision and the write, and drop the `await` from the critical section (or use an atomic increment-then-rollback):

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ try_consume checks and writes across an await without holding _lock

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Counters never decay, so LIMIT is a lifetime cap not a rate limit

Under concurrent calls for the same tenant, two coroutines can both read the same 'current' value, both pass the limit check, and both write, allowing the tenant to exceed LIMIT — exactly the race the rate limiter is meant to prevent. There is no test in this diff exercising concurrent calls to try_consume, so this bug would ship silently.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits `attempted` shares the same list object. Each call appends its failures to that shared list and returns it, so the second call returns its own failures *plus* every failure from all previous calls — callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will get a growing, wrong result (and the list grows unboundedly for the process lifetime).

Use `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` and then `attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted` at the top of the body.

findings.title: Retry around non-idempotent charge can double-charge customers
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge. Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure after the gateway has already accepted the request (timeout, dropped connection, 5xx on the response leg) causes a second and possibly third charge to be created. The customer is billed 2–3x with no way for the caller to detect it.

The gateway docstring states it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a stable key per logical charge attempt (e.g. derived from an order/payment id, not per-retry) and pass it through `charge()` so the gateway collapses retries into one charge. Only then is the retry decorator safe here. Alternatively, drop the retry on this path and reconcile via `get_charge`.

The retry on `fetch_charge` (line 5–7) is fine: `get_charge` is a documented-safe GET.

If a transient failure occurs after the gateway processed the charge (e.g., timeout on the response), the retry will create a second charge. Nothing in this diff exercises charge_card under a simulated flaky-then-success scenario to check that only one charge is created; a test asserting on retry.call_count or on the mocked charge() call count would not catch this since it would just confirm the function was called 3 times, not that duplicate real-world charges resulted.

findings.title: Unvalidated project query param reaches buildPath, enabling path traversal
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, is no longer checked by `common.ValidateID` before it flows on to the file DAO. The retrieved `buildPath` explicitly states: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." This hunk removes exactly that caller-side validation.

The justification that "the path join already scopes under the folder root" does not hold: `filepath.Join` applies `Clean`, which *resolves* `..` segments rather than rejecting them, so `filepath.Join("/data", "../../etc", kind)` yields `/etc/<kind>` — outside the storage root. A value such as `?project=../../..%2Fsomething` therefore escapes the folder root, and even without traversal an unconstrained name can be used to address documents the ID grammar was meant to exclude.

Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check (returning `HandleBadRequestError`) before the parameter is used, or push an equivalent validation into `buildPath` itself so the contract is enforced in one place.

findings.title: Buffer reserved from attacker-declared Content-Length before reading body
findings.body:
`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` sizes the buffer from `contentLength`, which for an S3 `UploadPart` request originates in the client-supplied `Content-Length` header (the parameter is passed in from the HTTP handler, see signature on line 2). Nothing in this function verifies that the declared length matches the bytes actually delivered, or that it is within any per-part limit — the `io.Copy` on line 8 only discovers the true size afterwards.

Consequences:

- A client can send `Content-Length: 5368709120` with a one-byte body and make the server commit gigabytes of heap per in-flight request. Repeating this across concurrent connections is a cheap remote OOM / denial of service; the attacker pays almost no bandwidth.
- If `contentLength` can be `-1` or `0` (chunked / unknown-length transfer encoding, which the previous growth-on-demand code handled naturally), `Reserve` is being called with a value it may not expect; depending on its implementation that is a panic or a silently wrong capacity.

Suggested fix: clamp before reserving, e.g. only reserve when `contentLength > 0`, cap it at the configured maximum part size (`min(contentLength, maxPartSize)`), and reject or fall back to incremental growth otherwise. Pair that with enforcing the declared length against the bytes actually copied so an over-declared part is rejected rather than silently accepted.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from attacker-declared Content-Length

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Reserve(contentLength) unguarded for unknown/negative length

findings.title: No test covers pre-reservation against actual body size
findings.body: The change now pre-allocates the multipart buffer using the caller-supplied contentLength via Reserve(contentLength). There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises the case where contentLength does not match the actual bytes read from body (e.g., a Content-Length larger or smaller than the real upload, or a very large declared length). If Reserve's behavior changes, or if it causes incorrect allocation/growth handling relative to the actual number of bytes copied, nothing would catch it — the existing io.Copy path just proceeds and returns n, err, and no assertion in the visible code path checks that pre-reservation had any effect or that mismatched lengths are handled safely.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The previous expression (`"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`) was a deliberate fail-secure default: TLS was used unless the caller explicitly opted out with `is_secure=False`. The new ternary treats every falsy value — including the common case where `is_secure` is simply absent from `request.meta` and `.get()` returns `None` — as a request for plaintext. Since `is_secure` is opt-in metadata that most callers never set, the effective default for all S3 downloads flips from HTTPS to HTTP.

The resulting URL on line 6 is the transport for requests that carry AWS authorization material (signature/date headers, and for the legacy v2 scheme an `AWSAccessKeyId`/`Signature` pair that can appear in the query string preserved on line 5). Anyone on the network path can read the object contents and replay or reuse the signed request.

Restore the fail-secure form, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, so that only an explicit `False` downgrades the connection.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Default S3 scheme flips from https to http when is_secure is unset

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ S3 scheme logic inverted: defaults now insecure

findings.title: Scheme-default change has no accompanying test
findings.body: The old logic defaulted to https unless is_secure was explicitly False; the new logic defaults to http unless is_secure is truthy. This changes behavior for the common case where is_secure is absent from request.meta (e.g. None or missing), switching the resulting URL from https to http. No test file is included in this diff, so if this default flip is unintended (a security-relevant regression), nothing would fail to signal it.

findings.title: DELETE now maps to "push", granting delete to push-only accounts
findings.body:
The removed `switch` mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the distinct action `"delete"`. The new condition only special-cases GET and HEAD, so DELETE falls into the `!= GET && != HEAD` branch and requests `"push"`.

Two consequences, both authorization failures:

1. Any account authorized for `push` on a repository can now delete tags/manifests, because the access check it is measured against is the push grant. The retrieved config comment states the separation is deliberate: "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones."
2. `ResourceAction.Action` is never `"delete"` any more, so existing policies that grant only `delete` no longer match anything and those accounts lose the ability they were configured for.

Keep the DELETE case explicit:

```go
action := "pull"
switch request.Method {
case http.MethodGet, http.MethodHead:
    action = "pull"
case http.MethodDelete:
    action = "delete"
default:
    action = "push"
}
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorised as "push"; delete permission check removed

findings.title: Action mapping no longer matches documented contract
findings.body: The code change collapses the three-action model (pull, push, delete) documented in pkg/api/config/config.go into a two-action model (pull, push). The DELETE HTTP method is no longer mapped to ActionDelete, but instead to ActionPush. The repository documentation explicitly states that 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' This change breaks that contract without updating the documentation, making callers who rely on the documented behavior incorrect.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE now mapping to push instead of delete
findings.body: The change collapses the previous three-way method-to-action mapping (pull/push/delete) into a two-way one, so HTTP DELETE requests now resolve to action "push" instead of "delete". Per the repo's own documented access model (pkg/api/config/config.go), pull/push/delete are intentionally distinct so an account can push without being able to delete. This diff contains no test changes, so if this mapping is wrong (e.g. it should have stayed "delete", or the collapse is an unintended regression), nothing in the test suite would fail. A test asserting that DELETE requests map to a specific action is needed to catch regressions here.

findings.title: Function name `get_tenant_fresh` is misleading about side effects
findings.body:
The function name `get_tenant_fresh` follows the `get_*` convention, which typically implies a read-only operation. However, this function has significant side effects: it modifies the shared `_CACHE` dictionary and clears it when it exceeds 1000 entries. A caller familiar with `get_tenant()` would reasonably expect `get_tenant_fresh()` to be a variant that bypasses the cache, not one that mutates it. The name should either (1) be changed to reflect that it mutates the cache (e.g., `fetch_and_cache_tenant`), or (2) the function should be documented with a docstring explaining the cache side effects. Without this, callers risk misusing the function or introducing unexpected cache clears.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Size guard clears the whole shared cache, discarding the fresh entry

findings.title: New get_tenant_fresh function has no test coverage
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces new behavior: it fetches fresh data, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. If the cache-write were wrong (e.g. wrong key, stale tenant object) or the eviction threshold/logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, clearing too aggressively, or never clearing causing unbounded growth), nothing would fail — the function would simply return whatever _fetch returns, masking the side-effect bugs.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id keys shared cache; 1000-entry clear flushes all tenants
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` uses `tenant_id` directly as the key of the module-level `_CACHE` (line 10) with no validation that the id is well-formed or that the caller may act on that tenant, and the eviction policy on lines 11-12 is a full `clear()` of the shared dict. If any request-facing caller passes a client-supplied id here, a caller can (a) insert an unbounded number of distinct keys, each holding whatever `_fetch` returns, and (b) by exceeding 1000 entries, evict every other tenant's cached entry at will, turning a cheap loop into repeated backing-store load for all tenants. Consider a bounded LRU (e.g. `functools.lru_cache` or an explicit LRU with per-key eviction instead of `clear()`), and validate/normalise `tenant_id` before it becomes a key. Note also that a `None` result from `_fetch` is cached, so a failed lookup for an unknown id persists as a negative entry that `get_tenant` cannot distinguish from a miss.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag under old name
findings.body:
The README.md still describes the flag as `--workers`, but cli.py now defines it as `--concurrency`. A user following the documentation will use the wrong flag name and the tool will fail. Update line 7 to use the new flag name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed --workers flag

findings.title: Renaming --workers changes args.workers to args.concurrency for all callers
findings.body:
`add_argument("--concurrency", ...)` makes argparse store the value under `args.concurrency`; the previous `--workers` stored it under `args.workers`. Any code that reads `args.workers` (or `getattr(ns, "workers")`) will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime rather than fail at import, so it will not be caught by a syntax or type check. Equally, any existing shell script, systemd unit, Makefile or CI job invoking `--workers` now exits with argparse's "unrecognized arguments" error.

If the rename is intended to be user-visible, grep for `\.workers` across the repo and update every consumer in this PR. If it is only meant to align the internal name, keep backwards compatibility instead: `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)` accepts both spellings while exposing a single attribute.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts new return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping day strings to counts. A caller relying on this docstring will attempt to use the result as an integer and fail. Update the docstring to reflect the new return contract: a dictionary with day identifiers as keys and call counts as values.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict without updating callers or docstring
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any existing caller doing arithmetic or comparison on the result (`monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `total + monthly_usage(a)`, formatting it into a message) will now either raise `TypeError` or silently produce a wrong result — comparing a dict to an int raises, but truthiness checks like `if monthly_usage(a):` will keep working while meaning something different. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so nothing in the code signals the break.

Either keep the scalar contract and add a new function (e.g. `monthly_usage_by_day`), or update the docstring and audit/adjust every call site in the same change.

findings.title: Return type change from int to dict has no accompanying test
findings.body: monthly_usage's return type and structure changed from a single integer total to a dict keyed by day. Any caller expecting an int (as documented in the now-stale docstring) would break, and no test in this diff verifies the new shape, keys, or aggregation correctness. If the GROUP BY query or dict construction were wrong (e.g., wrong key name, duplicate days, empty result set), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Docstring parameter name does not match signature
findings.body: The docstring on line 6 refers to `page_size`, but the function signature on line 1 now uses `limit`. A caller reading the docstring to understand the parameter would be confused, as the documented name does not appear in the actual function signature. Update the docstring to use the new parameter name `limit`.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a module-level function whose second parameter was renamed from `page_size` to `limit`. Any existing caller written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at call time — positional callers are unaffected, so the failure is silent until that specific code path runs. Either grep for and update all `page_size=` call sites in the same change, or keep backwards compatibility for a deprecation window, e.g. accept `page_size=None` via `**kwargs` and map it onto `limit` with a warning. Note also that the PR description says the rename is `page`  f `offset`, which does not match what the diff actually does; worth confirming the intended contract before landing.

findings.title: No test guards the renamed keyword parameter
findings.body: list_invoices' second parameter was renamed from page_size to limit. Any caller invoking list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=X, cursor=Y) as a keyword argument will now raise a TypeError instead of working. No test in this diff exercises the function with a keyword argument to catch that breakage, and no repository context was retrieved showing such a test exists elsewhere.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail to import
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, but this is an absolute import. Every other import in this file is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). Under Python 3 (and Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this raises `ImportError: No module named adapters` at import time of `requests.sessions`, i.e. the whole library fails to import. Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert accepted but silently dropped in new request() path
findings.body: The rewritten `request()` still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None` in its signature, but the body only copies method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request` before calling `req.prepare()` and `self.send(prep)`. Neither `verify` nor `cert` is attached to the request or passed to `send()`, and `send()` (line 365-367) constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` and calls `adapter.send(request)` with no TLS arguments. Any caller that pins a CA bundle (`verify='/path/ca.pem'`) or presents a client certificate (`cert=...`) now gets neither — the call succeeds while the control the caller asked for is simply not applied, which is the classic silent-downgrade-to-unverified-TLS shape and is exploitable by an active network attacker. The same is true of the session-level `config`/`trust_env` verification defaults, which the old `old_request` path (kept at line 172) still honours. Either thread `verify`/`cert` through `prepare()`/`send()` to the adapter, or raise `NotImplementedError` for these kwargs until the adapter wiring exists rather than accepting and ignoring them.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but still called by `old_request`
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper was removed in this diff, yet the retained `old_request` path still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches that line raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the helper until `old_request` is deleted, or inline the two-line body (`r.send(prefetch=...)`; `return r.response`) at the call site.

findings.title: New `request()` accepts timeout/verify/cert/prefetch/config but ignores them
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are bound and then dropped on the floor. These are not cosmetic: a caller doing `session.get(url, verify=False)` or `session.post(url, cert=(...))` now silently gets whatever the adapter defaults to, and `timeout=...` no longer bounds the request at all, so a hung peer blocks forever. `return_response=False` previously returned the un-sent request object; now line 167 unconditionally returns the send result, breaking that contract too. Either thread these through to `self.send(prep, ...)` or raise/`NotImplementedError` for the ones not yet wired up so the failure is loud.

findings.title: New HTTPAdapter per send plus no-op close drops all connection pooling
findings.body: `send()` constructs a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` on every call, so each request gets its own PoolManager and no socket is ever reused across requests on the same Session — the entire point of a Session. Compounding this, `close()` is now `pass`, so neither the old PoolManager nor the per-call adapters are ever cleared; `with Session() as s:` leaks every connection it opened. Hold a single adapter on the Session (created in `__init__` from `pool_connections`/`pool_maxsize`/`support_http0.9` as `init_poolmanager` used to) and have `close()` close it.

findings.title: Unqualified `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is shadowable
findings.body: Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). This one is absolute, so it resolves against `sys.path` rather than the `requests` package. On Python 3 it will not find the sibling module at all (ImportError at import time for the whole library), and on Python 2 / any environment where `sys.path[0]` is the working directory, it resolves to whatever top-level `adapters.py` happens to be importable first — meaning an attacker who can drop a file into the process's working directory or any earlier `sys.path` entry gets arbitrary code execution inside the HTTP client that also handles credentials and TLS settings. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: close() is now a no-op with no test to catch regressed resource cleanup
findings.body: close() previously closed the PoolManager and its pooled connections; it is now `pass`. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises Session.close() to confirm connections are actually released now that pooling has moved off the Session. If the PoolManager/adapter is supposed to be closed elsewhere, nothing here verifies that happens, so a resource leak introduced by this refactor would go undetected.

findings.title: New send() delegates to HTTPAdapter with no test covering the new path
findings.body: Session.send() previously called request.send() directly; it now constructs an HTTPAdapter per call and delegates to it. This is the core of the described refactor (moving sending onto an HTTPAdapter) but no test in the diff verifies that requests are actually sent/received correctly through the new adapter path, or that a Response is returned as before. If HTTPAdapter.send() is broken or returns the wrong type, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Removed docstring on close() without explanation
findings.body: The close() method's docstring explained that it "disposes of any internal state" by closing the PoolManager and its pooled connections. This docstring is removed and the method now does nothing (pass). This is misleading to callers who expect close() to release resources. Either the docstring should remain (even if the implementation changes), or a comment should explain why close() is now a no-op during this refactor.

findings.title: send() method contract change undocumented
findings.body: The send() method's docstring says 'Send a given PreparedRequest.' but the implementation changes from 'return request.send()' (delegating to the request object) to creating an HTTPAdapter and calling 'adapter.send(request)'. This is a significant behavioral change in how the request is dispatched. The docstring does not document that an HTTPAdapter is now involved, which matters for understanding where request handling happens and for future maintainers.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header makes cookies property return None, crashing callers
findings.body:
Entry point: the client-controlled `Cookie` request header. Sink: `Cookie.SimpleCookie.load()` on line 520. If `load()` raises (Python 2's `Cookie` module raises `CookieError` on a variety of malformed inputs), the handler sets `self._cookies = None` and line 524 returns `None`.

Every consumer assumes a mapping: `web.py:321` does `if name in self.request.cookies`, and `web.py:367` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()`. Both raise `TypeError` on `None`, producing an unhandled 500 for any request that touches cookies — which includes `get_secure_cookie`/XSRF paths. That is a trivially remote-triggerable denial of service (one bad header per request, no auth needed), and with `debug=True` the resulting traceback is rendered to the client.

The previous implementation avoided this: on failure it called `clear_all_cookies()` and still returned the (partially populated) `SimpleCookie`, so the return value was always a mapping. Restore that invariant, e.g. set `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()` in the `except` branch rather than `None`. Note also that dropping the `clear_all_cookies()` call means the malformed cookie is no longer expired in the client's browser, so the failure repeats on every subsequent request from that client.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ cookies returns None on parse failure, breaking all consumers

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed with no delegating alias
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a public, documented property; application subclasses and templates commonly read `self.cookies` / `handler.cookies` directly. Deleting it without leaving `@property def cookies(self): return self.request.cookies` turns every such use into an `AttributeError` at runtime rather than a deprecation. Keep a one-line delegating property on `RequestHandler` alongside the new `HTTPRequest.cookies`.

findings.title: Untested behaviour change in cookie-parse failure path
findings.body: The moved `cookies` property changes what happens when `Cookie.SimpleCookie().load()` raises: previously (in web.py) the handler called `self.clear_all_cookies()` on failure, leaving `self.cookies` as an (empty) SimpleCookie instance; now `self._cookies` is set to `None`. Any caller of `request.cookies` (e.g. `get_cookie`'s `name in self.request.cookies`, or `clear_all_cookies`'s `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()`) will now raise a TypeError/AttributeError on a malformed Cookie header instead of behaving as before. No test exercises a malformed Cookie header for either the old or new code path, so this behavioural change would go undetected.

findings.title: Cookie parsing failure behavior differs from RequestHandler but is undocumented
findings.body: The old `RequestHandler.cookies` property (in tornado/web.py) called `self.clear_all_cookies()` when cookie parsing failed. The new `HTTPRequest.cookies` property silently sets `self._cookies = None`. This behavioral change should be documented in the docstring so callers understand what happens when cookie headers are malformed.

findings.title: Missing strip() makes boundary lookup fail for normal headers
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields parameter segments that keep the whitespace after the separator, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc"` produces the segment `" boundary=----abc"`. `field.partition("=")` then sets `k` to `" boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the `break` is never reached, the `for ... else` clause runs and logs "Invalid multipart/form-data", and `_parse_mime_body` is never called. Every multipart upload from a client that emits the customary space after the semicolon (i.e. essentially all of them) now loses its form data — the previous `'boundary=' in content_type` test was whitespace-insensitive and did not have this problem. Use `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. While there, consider `v.strip('"')` since RFC 2046 permits a quoted boundary value.

findings.title: Content-Type parameters not stripped; boundary never matches
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the conventional leading space, e.g. `" boundary=abc"` for the standard header `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc`. `field.partition("=")` then gives `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop falls through to the `for/else` and every well-formed multipart request is logged as "Invalid multipart/form-data" and silently discarded — a regression against the previous `'boundary=' in content_type` substring check. Use `field.strip().partition("=")`.

While touching this: RFC 2045 permits a quoted parameter value (`boundary="abc"`), and the quotes are passed through to `_parse_mime_body` verbatim here, which will also fail to find the delimiter. Stripping surrounding double quotes from `v` would make the parse robust.

Security-wise this fails closed (no body arguments/files are populated) rather than open, so I am not rating it as a vulnerability; the entry point is the client-supplied `Content-Type` header and the sink is `_parse_mime_body`, where the value is used as a literal delimiter, not fed to an interpreter.

findings.title: No test coverage for new multipart boundary-parsing logic
findings.body: The change alters how the boundary parameter is extracted from Content-Type (now scanning all `;`-separated fields instead of assuming boundary is last), but no test exercises this code path. In particular, `field.partition('=')` does not strip whitespace, so a Content-Type like `multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz` (space before 'boundary') would produce k=' boundary' which fails the `k == "boundary"` check — silently causing multipart bodies to be skipped as invalid. Nothing in the diff or any visible test would catch this regression. A test with boundary in a non-last position (the stated motivation for the fix) and one with a leading space after `;` should be added to confirm both the fix and its edge cases.

findings.title: get_host authority parsing ignores '?' and '#', allowing host confusion
findings.body:
`get_host` terminates the authority component only on `/` (line 92). Per RFC 3986 the authority also ends at the first `?` or `#`. Because the `@` split (line 94) runs over whatever is left, a URL like `http://google.com?@evil.com/` or `http://google.com#@evil.com/` is parsed here as host `evil.com`, while `urllib.parse.urlsplit` — and anything else doing allowlist checks — reports `google.com`. The same applies to a backslash, which several clients normalise to `/` but this parser does not.

If any caller (or downstream consumer of this public helper) feeds a user-supplied URL through `get_host` to pick a connection target, or checks the returned host against an allowlist, the two parsers disagree and the request goes to the attacker's host. Suggest stripping at the first occurrence of any of `/?#` before the userinfo split, or delegating to `urlsplit` and keeping this only as a fast path.

I cannot see the callers in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm an exploitable SSRF path here — the defect is in the parser itself.

findings.title: New util.py helpers have no accompanying tests
findings.body: This PR moves/introduces make_headers, get_host, and is_connection_dropped into a new module but the diff contains no test file. In particular get_host's branching logic (scheme/path/auth/port parsing and the LocationParseError raised when port is non-numeric at line 100) and is_connection_dropped's two platform-specific code paths (poll vs select) are behaviour with real edge cases that nothing here would catch if broken by a future change — e.g. the malformed error message `"Failed to parse: %s"` with no `% port` substitution would go unnoticed. If tests for these already exist elsewhere in the repo and were simply not touched, this is lower priority; but as presented, this change introduces untested logic.

findings.title: LocationParseError message never interpolates the URL
findings.body: `"Failed to parse: %s"` is raised with no `% url` applied, so the exception text is the literal string containing `%s` and the caller loses the only piece of diagnostic information the error carries. Change to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (note `url` has already been truncated by the earlier splits, so consider capturing the original argument if the full URL is wanted).

findings.title: is_connection_dropped assumes conn.sock is a live socket
findings.body: `conn.sock` is `None` on an `HTTPConnection` that has been constructed but never connected (httplib sets `self.sock = None` in `__init__`). In that state `select([None], [], [], 0.0)` raises `TypeError` and `p.register(None, POLLIN)` raises as well, so a pool that hands out a freshly created, never-used connection will blow up here instead of reporting "not dropped". Guard with something like `sock = getattr(conn, 'sock', None)` / `if not sock: return False` before the poll/select. Also note the poll branch falls off the end and returns `None` rather than `False`; harmless in a boolean test but inconsistent with the documented return value.

findings.title: Sorting by "status" column is untested
findings.body: SORTABLE now maps three keys (created_at, amount, status), but only created_at (via default) and amount are exercised by tests. If the status column mapping were wrong (e.g. typo'd to a nonexistent column, or mismapped to the wrong DB column), no test would catch it.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now returns URL object, not string
findings.body:
The documentation in docs/web_reference.rst states that `HTTPMove.location` is 'the string it was constructed with' and that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to str.startswith'. However, this diff changes `self.location` to store a `URL(location)` object instead of the original string. Code expecting a string and calling methods like `str.startswith()` directly on `self.location` will now fail. Either update the documentation to reflect that `location` is now a URL object, or revert to storing the string and only converting to URL for the header.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location attribute type change can silently break redirect allowlist checks

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ HTTPMove.location now a URL object, breaking documented string contract

findings.title: No test guards location's documented str type/behavior
findings.body: `self.location` is now assigned `URL(location)` instead of the original string, changing its public type from `str` to `yarl.URL`. Documentation states the attribute should be 'the string it was constructed with' and used with `str.startswith`. Nothing in this diff (no test file present) exercises `exc.location` to confirm it is still a string or behaves like one (e.g. supports `startswith`), so this behavior change would go undetected by the test suite.

findings.title: `if` instead of `while` lets readany() return b'' before EOF
findings.body:
`_wait()` documents that the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, and explicitly requires the caller to re-check its condition after waking. Replacing the `while` loop with `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a spurious/chunk-boundary wake, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and no EOF, so `readany()` returns `b''`.

Callers of `readany()` (and the `async for` / chunked-iteration paths built on it) treat an empty `bytes` return as end-of-stream, so this silently truncates the body instead of continuing to wait. Restore the loop:

```python
while not self._buffer and not self._eof:
    await self._wait('readany')
```

If the intent really is a single wake, the empty-result case must be handled explicitly rather than falling through to `_read_nowait`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ readany() can return empty bytes as false EOF after a spurious wake

findings.title: No test exercises spurious-wake retry behavior for readany
findings.body: The change from `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` to `if not self._buffer and not self._eof` removes the retry loop that re-checks the wait condition after waking. Per the docstring on `_wait`, the waiter can resolve 'at the end of a chunk' with no new data, meaning a caller must re-check its condition — which is exactly what the `while` loop did. With `if`, a spurious wake with an empty buffer and no eof will fall through to `_read_nowait(-1)` and likely return no data prematurely instead of waiting again. No test in the diff or visible repo context exercises this multi-wake/no-data scenario, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks package import on Python 3
findings.body:
`from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328 / `absolute_import`), so on Python 3 this line raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` and importing `requests.sessions` 	odd fails outright 	odd taking the whole package with it, since `Session`/`HTTPAdapter` are re-exported from here. Even on Python 2 it is not equivalent: if a top-level `adapters` module exists anywhere on `sys.path`, that one wins over `requests/adapters.py`, silently binding a different `HTTPAdapter`. Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Import change breaks relative import contract

findings.title: Implicit import lets a top-level `adapters` module hijack HTTPAdapter
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously resolves to the sibling module inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is resolved against `sys.path` on Python 3 (and on Python 2 only falls back to the sibling because implicit relative imports are still enabled there). That means whichever `adapters.py`/`adapters/` appears first on `sys.path` wins — and `sys.path[0]` is the invoking script's directory, which for many deployments is a writable or user-controlled location. Anyone who can place an `adapters.py` there gets arbitrary code executed at import time inside every process that imports `requests.sessions`, and gets to substitute their own `HTTPAdapter` (i.e. control the transport layer: TLS verification, proxying, request bodies) for all HTTP traffic in the process.

There is no behavioural benefit to the change; the adjacent line 6 (`from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`) already uses the explicit-relative house form. Revert to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Removing None guard makes get_cookie raise on unparsable Cookie header
findings.body:
The PR description claims "cookies is always a mapping after construction", but the `cookies` property in `tornado/httpserver.py` documents and implements the opposite: it returns `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, and the docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, raising `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` for any request carrying a malformed Cookie header — an attacker-or-client-controlled input that turns a benign `default` return into a 500. Restore the guard (`if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`), or alternatively change the property to return `{}` instead of `None` — but that is a separate contract change affecting all other consumers.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header raise TypeError

findings.title: get_cookie now breaks documented contract of cookies property
findings.body: The get_cookie method now assumes self.request.cookies is never None, but the cookies property docstring (in httpserver.py) explicitly documents: "Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that." Removing the None-check means get_cookie will raise TypeError when cookies is None and name is checked against it. This violates the documented API contract that all consumers must handle None.

findings.body: The retrieved cookies property docstring explicitly states cookies is set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, and 'every consumer has to allow for that.' The diff removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` guard from get_cookie, which would raise a TypeError ('argument of type NoneType is not iterable') if this documented scenario occurs. There's no test in this change exercising get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Dropping strip() makes multipart boundary parsing silently fail
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the conventional leading space, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=abc"` -> `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=abc"]`. Previously `field.strip()` removed that space so `k == "boundary"` matched. Without the strip, `k` is `" boundary"` and the equality on line 5 is never true, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called and the request body is silently discarded — all multipart form uploads stop producing arguments/files, with no error raised. The strip also normalised trailing whitespace/CR in the value passed as the boundary on line 6. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (or at minimum `k.strip()`/`v.strip()`); the strip was not redundant.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection and allows parser differential
findings.body:
Entry point: the attacker/client-controlled `Content-Type` request header. Sink: `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)`, which uses `v` as the MIME part delimiter.

Two concrete consequences of removing `field.strip()`:

1. For the standard header form `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc`, `content_type.split(";")` yields `" boundary=abc"`. Without the strip, `partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, and `_parse_mime_body` is never called. Multipart bodies are silently discarded — no error, no log — so handlers see empty `arguments`/`files`. Anything that depends on body content being present (XSRF token lookup, per-field authorisation or validation in handlers) now operates on an empty body, and a front-end proxy/WAF that *does* parse the body will disagree with what the application sees.

2. For the no-space form `multipart/form-data;boundary=abc \t`, the trailing whitespace previously removed by the strip is now kept in `v` and passed to `_parse_mime_body` as the delimiter. Tornado will look for `--abc \t` while a strictly-parsing intermediary looks for `--abc`, giving an attacker a way to make the two components segment the same body differently.

Restore the strip on the whole parameter (`field.strip().partition("=")`), or at minimum strip both `k` and `v`. Note also that the PR description says the removed strip was on "the parameter value" — it was applied to the whole `key=value` parameter, which is why the key is affected.

findings.title: No test guards boundary parsing after removing strip()
findings.body: The change removes `.strip()` before partitioning on '=', so a field like ' boundary=xyz' (with leading space, as typically produced by splitting 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' on ';') now yields k == ' boundary' instead of 'boundary', which fails the `k == "boundary"` check on line 5. This is a real behavioral change to a commonly-used code path (multipart form parsing), yet no test file is included in this diff. If this introduced a regression, nothing in the current test suite (not shown, and not modified here) would catch it.

findings.title: Format placeholder left in message with no argument
findings.body: The string still contains the `%s` placeholder but the `% url` interpolation was removed, so the exception message is the literal text `Failed to parse: %s`. The URL that failed to parse is no longer reported, which makes the error useless for diagnosis and looks like a formatting bug to anyone reading logs. If the goal was to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too (e.g. `LocationParseError(url)` or a fixed string without `%s`); if the URL should be retained, restore `% url`.

findings.title: Unquoted f-string interpolated into shell=True command
findings.body:
`cmd` is built by interpolating `name` and `directory` directly into a string that is then executed with `shell=True`. Two concrete failures: (1) correctness — a `directory` or `name` containing a space is split into multiple shell words, so `create_archive("my backup", "/data")` writes `/exports/my` and tars `backup.tar.gz` plus `/data`; (2) security — a metacharacter such as `;`, `&&`, `$(...)` or a backtick in either argument executes arbitrary commands as the service user. The sibling `list_exports` on line 5 already uses the safe list form. Match it: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz"), directory], check=True)` with no `shell=True`, and validate that `name` contains no path separators so it cannot escape `/exports` via `../`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Command injection via shell=True in create_archive

findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function's behavior (e.g., verifying the tarball is created, that arguments are handled safely, or that malformed names are rejected). Since this is a new code path with security-sensitive shell execution, an untested regression (e.g., broken quoting, wrong flags, or unsafe input) would go unnoticed.

findings.body: `list_exports` returns `.stdout` (bytes), while `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess` object. Callers of this module will reasonably expect a consistent convention. Either return `.stdout` (adding `capture_output=True`) or return nothing and let `check=True` signal failure, but pick one and match the module.

findings.title: Public function `create_archive` lacks documentation
findings.body: The `create_archive` function is a public API that takes user-controlled parameters (`name` and `directory`) and constructs a shell command with them. Without a docstring, callers cannot see what constraints apply to these parameters or what the function returns. Add a docstring that documents: (1) what each parameter is and any constraints on its format, (2) what the function returns, and (3) what exceptions it may raise.

findings.title: CORS allowlist widened to `*` while credentials remain enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, bypassing the `ALLOWED` allowlist used by the existing export two lines above. Entry point: a cross-origin HTTP request from any website a logged-in user visits, carrying their session cookie. Sink: the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers emitted by this middleware on whatever routes mount it — which then let the attacker's page read authenticated API responses.

Two outcomes, both bad:
- If the underlying `cors` helper emits the literal `*`, browsers reject the credentialed response and the dashboard simply will not work — the stated goal is not met, and someone will "fix" it by reflecting the Origin header, which is the full vulnerability.
- If this helper (or any wrapper around it) reflects the request `Origin` instead of emitting a literal `*`, every origin on the internet is trusted with cookies right now.

Fix: name the dashboard origin explicitly, e.g. add it to `ALLOWED` and reuse the existing export, or `origin: ["https://dashboard.example.com"]`. Never combine a wildcard or an unconditional Origin reflection with `credentials: true`.

findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*" })` emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. When a request is made with `credentials: 'include'` (the whole point of `credentials: true` here), the browser refuses to expose the response and fails the request — the wildcard is not permitted in a credentialed response. So this middleware does not achieve what the PR describes: the dashboard still cannot call the API with cookies, and preflights will fail too.

Use an explicit origin (or a reflecting function/allowlist, as the existing `ALLOWED` config on line 6 appears to do) so a concrete origin value is echoed back, e.g. `origin: DASHBOARD_ORIGIN` or extend `ALLOWED` to include the dashboard origin rather than adding a second middleware. As a side effect this also avoids widening the API to every origin.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ CORS configuration violates spec: wildcard origin + credentials

findings.title: New dashboardCors config has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, a configuration that most CORS middleware implementations reject or silently disable at runtime (browsers refuse wildcard origin with credentials). There is no test verifying what the middleware actually does with this configuration — e.g. what `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header value is produced, or whether requests with credentials succeed. If this configuration is broken or behaves unexpectedly, nothing in the current change would surface it.

findings.title: Public CORS export lacks documentation of purpose and security model
findings.body: The `dashboardCors` export is a public API (it is exported at module level) with a CORS configuration that combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`. This combination is unusual and contradictory at the protocol level—credentials (cookies) cannot be sent to wildcard origins per the CORS spec. A caller examining the code would reasonably be confused about what this actually does and whether it is the intended behavior. Add a comment explaining the purpose of this export, which dashboard it serves, and clarify whether the credential setting is intentional or a mistake.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is now a literal in the repository and is assigned directly to `acmepay.api_key`. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production (not test) credential. Anyone with read access to the repo, to any fork or clone, to CI logs that echo the file, or to a built artifact now holds a key that can move real money through the payments provider. Removing `import os` also deletes the only mechanism by which the key was kept out of version control, so there is no longer an environment-based override.

Actions: (1) treat the key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay immediately — deleting the line does not undo exposure, since it remains in git history; (2) restore `acmepay.api_key = os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` (or read from your secret manager); (3) scrub history / revoke as your incident process requires; (4) consider adding a secret-scanning pre-commit hook so the next one is caught before merge.

findings.title: client() ignores ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY; all environments use one live key
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the API key at call time from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which is what let staging, CI and production each point at their own AcmePay account. After this change the environment variable is never read and every caller of `client()` gets the same `acme_live_...` key baked into the module. Any deployment or test run that was relying on exporting `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` with a test key will silently begin issuing real charges against the live account, with no error to signal the misconfiguration. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit failure when unset) rather than a module-level constant.

findings.title: client() function contract no longer documented
findings.body: The `client()` function previously read the API key from an environment variable (line 8 in the old code: `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`), which was self-documenting behavior. It now reads from a module-level constant instead. This is a change to the public contract of this function that a caller or maintainer needs to understand. Either add a docstring explaining where the key comes from, or restore the documented behavior.

findings.title: No test exercises client() to catch the credential-source change
findings.body: The diff adds tests/fixtures/acmepay.py, but it only defines a fake_client() fixture and TEST_KEY constant — no test actually calls client() and asserts what acmepay.api_key is set to. If client() were reverted to read from an environment variable, or set to any other value, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module, whose key is read as the attribute `acmepay.api_key`. `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`. If this fixture is substituted for `client()` in tests, any code doing attribute access (`c.api_key`) or calling module-level functions on the result will fail or, worse, the fixture will only work for the narrow subset of tests that happen to use subscript access — giving false confidence that the real client is exercised. Consider returning a stub object exposing `api_key` as an attribute (e.g. `SimpleNamespace(api_key=TEST_KEY)`) so it is substitutable for the real return value.

findings.title: tenant_of() trusts an unverified JWT for tenant identity
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `tenant_id` from the result. Nothing authenticates the token, so any caller that uses this value to scope data access will honour whatever tenant id the client chose to put in the payload — a forged or self-issued token with an arbitrary `tenant_id` is accepted verbatim. In PyJWT, turning off `verify_signature` also switches off the other registered-claim checks (`exp`, `nbf`, `aud`), so expired tokens pass too.

Contrast with `claims_for()` on line 7, which verifies against `public_key()` with a pinned algorithm. `tenant_of()` should do the same and read the claim off the verified payload: `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the goal was to avoid the key-store round-trip, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_of() reads tenant_id from an unverified JWT

findings.title: Public function name obscures unverified token processing
findings.body: The function `tenant_of(token)` performs JWT decoding without signature verification (line 11 sets `verify_signature: False`). A caller reading this function name would reasonably assume it extracts the tenant from a validated token, paralleling the nearby `claims_for()` function that does verify. Without a docstring or name clarifying that the token is unverified, callers may use this to make authorization decisions on untrusted data. Either document explicitly that this returns unverified claims, or rename to `tenant_of_unverified(token)` to surface the risk.

findings.title: No test exercises tenant_of()'s unverified-decode behavior
findings.body: tenant_of() introduces a new code path that decodes the JWT without verifying its signature (verify_signature: False) and trusts the tenant_id claim as-is. No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if this function returned the wrong tenant, accepted a forged/unsigned token, or if the behavior were later 'fixed' to verify the signature and callers broke. Given this is a security-sensitive trust decision (tenant identification), at minimum a test should assert that a token with a tampered/unsigned payload still yields the claimed tenant (documenting the trust boundary) and that a token missing tenant_id raises rather than silently passing.

findings.title: Unhandled KeyError when the token carries no tenant_id claim
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` raises `KeyError` for any token that lacks the claim — which, since the payload is unauthenticated, an anonymous caller can trigger at will. Callers of `tenant_of()` will see a bare `KeyError` rather than an auth failure, which typically surfaces as a 500 instead of a 401/403. Use `.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the module's own auth error.

findings.title: Missing require_owner check lets any user update another's payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm` directly from the caller-supplied `pm_id` (line 12) and writes to it (lines 13-14) without any ownership check. `current_user(request)` on line 11 only authenticates — the retrieved `api/auth.py` states explicitly "Authentication only — never authorisation" and "Every object mutation must call this" for `require_owner`. The `user` variable is in fact assigned and then never used, which is the tell that the check was dropped.

Any signed-in user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and overwrite the `billing_name` on payment methods belonging to other accounts.

Fix: add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, before any mutation, mirroring line 6 in the read handler.

findings.title: Public mutation endpoint missing authorization contract documentation
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a public API endpoint that mutates a PaymentMethod object (line 14: `pm.save()`), but it lacks both the authorization check and any documentation explaining why authorization is omitted. The repository convention—established by the `require_owner` helper and its docstring stating 'Every object mutation must call this'—indicates this is a required safety pattern. Either add the `require_owner(user, pm)` call that this function is missing, or add a docstring explaining why this mutation does not need authorization.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is an unauthenticated handler that takes an attacker-supplied `email` and calls `send_reset_email(email)` with no remaining throttle. With the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator gone, an attacker can:

- flood any known address with reset mails (mail-bombing / harassment, and burning the sender's reputation and quota),
- enumerate accounts at high volume if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown addresses,
- generate an unbounded number of live reset tokens for a target account, widening the window for token guessing or interception.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — is a different control at a different layer: provider throttling protects the provider's sending infrastructure (typically a global or per-sender cap), not the per-recipient or per-source-IP cap that prevents targeted abuse, and hitting it degrades reset delivery for all users rather than blocking the abuser. If the decorator must go, replace it with an equivalent per-IP *and* per-target-email limit (e.g. middleware or a limiter inside `send_reset_email`) rather than removing the protection outright.

findings.title: Removal of rate limiting on password reset has no test coverage
findings.body: The rate_limit decorator on request_reset was removed with no accompanying test changes. If a test previously asserted rate-limiting behavior (e.g., 6th request in an hour is rejected), it should have failed after this change; since no test file is included in this diff, it's unclear whether such a test existed and was also removed, or whether this behavior was never covered. Either way, nothing in the current change would catch a regression if rate limiting should have been preserved.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file reads
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` joins the caller-supplied `name` directly onto `EXPORT_ROOT` rather than routing it through `_confined()`, which the download path on line 14 uses for the same input. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` containing `../` segments walks out of `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/passwd`) discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely, so the first `limit` bytes of any readable file are returned to the caller. Change line 20 to `path = _confined(name)` so preview and download share identical containment semantics, as the PR description claims they do.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path bypasses _confined(), enabling path traversal

findings.body: The function `read_export_preview(name, limit=4096)` accepts a `name` parameter and passes it directly to `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` without the `_confined()` safety check. The adjacent `read_export(name)` function applies `_confined()` on line 14, establishing a pattern that callers may reasonably expect this function to follow. If `read_export_preview` is intended to have different path semantics, this must be documented. If it should be confined like `read_export`, the implementation is a defect in the API contract itself (which would be caught by another reviewer), but the lack of any docstring makes the contract ambiguous to callers.

findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with a plain os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) instead of the _confined() helper used at line 14 for the download path. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a path-traversal-style regression (e.g. name containing '../') would not be caught. Since sibling read_export (download) is presumably tested against confinement, this new sibling function's divergent behavior is untested.

findings.title: bulk_export no longer enforces per-report ownership (cross-tenant IDOR)
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes caller-supplied `report_ids`, loads every `Report` by raw id (line 6) and returns its full serialisation (line 7). The loop that called `require_owner(user, report)` for each object was deleted, and `require_owner` was dropped from the import on line 1. `user` is now computed on line 5 and never used for any decision.

Authentication is not authorisation — any authenticated user of any tenant can now read arbitrary reports by guessing or enumerating ids. Restore the check, e.g. keep the `require_owner` import and loop, or better, scope the fetch itself to the caller's tenant (`Report.get(rid, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) so the filter cannot be dropped again. If the loop was the performance problem, batch-load the reports and compare `tenant_id` in one pass rather than removing the control.

findings.title: Public API now lacks documented authorization guarantees
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function is a public endpoint (takes `request` and `report_ids` parameters, returns data) but has no docstring. The change removes the per-object ownership check that was the only enforcement of the implicit contract that users can only export their own reports. Without documentation of this security boundary, or explicit enforcement, callers cannot know whether the endpoint is safe to use with untrusted input. Either restore the check, or add a docstring that explicitly states the authorization model (e.g., "Returns reports belonging to any tenant; caller must validate ownership before calling").

findings.title: No test would catch removal of ownership check in bulk_export
findings.body: The diff removes the per-report require_owner(user, report) authorization check from bulk_export. findings.body: If `Report.get(rid)` returns `None` for an unknown ID, `r.to_dict()` raises `AttributeError` and the endpoint 500s. Previously `require_owner(None, ...)` would have failed on `obj.tenant_id` first, so this was always fragile, but the removed loop at least gave a consistent failure point. findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameter contract
findings.body:
`billing/db.py.execute` documents "`params` must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows it by passing `%s` plus a tuple. `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params at all.

Two concrete failures follow from this, both reachable from normal support-desk input:

1. Any value containing a single quote terminates the literal early. Searching for `O'Brien` produces `... name LIKE '%O'Brien%' ...`, which is a syntax error, and a value chosen deliberately rewrites the statement outright.
2. `None` for either argument stringifies to the literal `'None'` rather than being rejected or treated as NULL, so the query silently returns the wrong (empty) result set instead of failing.

Fix by keeping the values out of the SQL text, matching line 5:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards move into the parameter value, which is where they belong once the literal quoting is gone.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
No test coverage for search_customers SQL construction
findings.body: search_customers builds its SQL via f-string interpolation instead of using execute's parameterised form (as get_customer does). There is no test in this diff that would catch this — a test asserting the query is parameterised (e.g. checking that term/status are passed as params rather than embedded in the SQL string) would have caught the injection risk. Since nothing exercises this function, a regression or the current defect would pass silently.

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of parameter contracts
findings.body: The `search_customers` function is exported from a module and takes user-supplied input (term, status) as parameters, but carries no docstring explaining what each parameter represents, what format is expected, or what the function returns. A caller reading only the function signature could not reliably use it correctly.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the send path enforces
findings.body:
The existing send path parses the URL and rejects it unless the host is in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before calling `requests.post`. `verify_endpoint` takes the same tenant-supplied URL and calls `requests.get` on it with no such check, so any caller that registers a webhook target can drive an authenticated server-side GET to an arbitrary host (internal services, link-local metadata endpoints) and read back the status code. Apply the same host extraction and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` membership check here before issuing the request — ideally by factoring lines 8-9 into a shared `_check_destination(url)` helper used by both functions — and pass `allow_redirects=False` so a permitted host cannot redirect the request to a denied one.
