findings.title: bulk_export no longer enforces per-object ownership (cross-tenant IDOR)
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes caller-supplied `report_ids`, loads each `Report` by ID, and serialises it with `to_dict()`. The loop calling `require_owner(user, report)` was deleted and the import of `require_owner` removed, so nothing now ties the fetched reports to `user.tenant_id`. Any authenticated caller can enumerate or guess report IDs and read other tenants' reports in bulk — authentication via `current_user` establishes who the caller is, not what they may read.

Restore the check, or push it into the query so it is not an O(n) round trip: fetch with a tenant filter (e.g. `Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) and fail or omit when the returned set does not match the requested IDs. If the loop was the performance problem, a single batched, tenant-scoped query solves both concerns; dropping the control does not.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-object ownership

findings.title: No test guards cross-tenant access in bulk_export
findings.body: The diff removes the per-report ownership check (`require_owner`) from `bulk_export` with no accompanying test change. If a test previously verified that `bulk_export` raises Forbidden for reports outside the caller's tenant, it is not shown here and would presumably now fail — but if no such test exists, this authorization regression would ship completely undetected. Since this is the core behavior change in the diff, a test asserting that `bulk_export` denies access to another tenant's report IDs is needed to catch this class of regression.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameter contract
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that it runs a *parameterised* query and that "`params` must carry every caller value". `search_customers` instead formats `term` and `status` straight into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with `params` omitted (defaulting to `None`). The neighbouring `get_customer` on line 5 follows the contract correctly.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is broken for perfectly ordinary input: a `term` of `O'Brien` closes the literal early and the driver raises a syntax error, and a `term` containing `%` or `_` silently changes the LIKE pattern so the search returns the wrong rows. A `term` or `status` of `None` interpolates the four characters `None` rather than matching NULL.

Fix by keeping the wildcards in the parameter value, not the SQL:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

findings.title: Public function violates documented contract of execute()
findings.body: The `execute()` helper in db.py is documented as requiring parameterised queries: "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." The new `search_customers()` function calls `execute(sql)` with only a raw SQL string containing unsanitised user input (`term` and `status`), passing no `params` argument. This directly contradicts the documented requirement and violates the API contract callers are supposed to follow.

findings.title: No test exercises search_customers
findings.body: search_customers is new behavior with no accompanying test in this diff. A test invoking it with sample term/status and asserting the resulting SQL/params (or a fake DB call) would catch both logic errors and the unparameterized query construction. Nothing here would fail if the function were subtly wrong (e.g., wrong operator, missing status filter, or SQL malformed).

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check (SSRF)
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` issues `requests.get(url, timeout=5)` with no validation, while the function immediately above it parses the host and rejects anything outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before sending. Per the PR description the URL being verified is the tenant-registered webhook target, i.e. attacker-supplied. A tenant can point it at `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...`, `http://localhost:port/...`, or any internal service and use the returned status code as an oracle to port-scan and fingerprint the internal network from the application's network position.

Apply the same host allowlist here \u2014 factor the `urlparse` + `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check into a shared `_check_destination(url)` and call it from both paths. Also consider `allow_redirects=False`, since a redirect from an allowlisted host otherwise re-opens the same hole, and reject non-http(s) schemes.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the send path enforces

findings.title: verify_endpoint return contract: truthy on 404, raises on transport failure
findings.body: For a function named `verify_endpoint`, returning the raw status code is a trap in two directions. A caller writing `if verify_endpoint(url):` gets a truthy value for 404, 500 and every other failure, since any status code is non-zero. And a connection refusal, DNS failure or timeout does not produce a status code at all \u2014 it raises `requests.RequestException` out of the function, so the caller must handle both an int and an exception to learn the same fact. Consider returning a bool (`200 <= code < 300`) with the transport errors caught and mapped to `False`, or document clearly that the caller owns exception handling.

findings.title: New verify_endpoint function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that makes an outbound GET request without the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used by the sibling POST function above it. There is no test in this diff verifying its behavior (e.g. that it returns a status code, or that it validates the host like the existing send function does). If this function were later found to skip host validation entirely, or to mishandle non-2xx/connection errors, nothing would catch it.

findings.title: Customer-invoice bucket ships with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is paired with a public access block that sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false`. That is the account-level guardrail that stops an S3 bucket holding customer billing data from ever being exposed by a bucket policy or object ACL, and this turns it off for that specific bucket. Nothing else in the diff grants public read, so the data is not necessarily reachable today — but any subsequent `aws_s3_bucket_policy`, any `public-read` object ACL set by an uploader, or any principal holding `s3:PutBucketPolicy`/`s3:PutObjectAcl` now makes invoices world-readable with no second control in the way. The bucket name is also globally predictable, so discovery is trivial once anything is exposed.

Remove the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` overrides and leave all four settings at `true` (the secure default). If the marketing site genuinely needs public objects, keep that scoped to `aws_s3_bucket.assets` and serve it via CloudFront with OAC rather than a public bucket. Also worth flagging separately: this resource is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR ("public assets bucket for the marketing site"), so it is likely to be waved through by a reviewer reading only the description.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket disables all four public-access protections

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with `==` instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` is a copy of `verify_stripe` except that the final comparison uses `expected == header`. Python's string `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks a prefix-match length and lets an attacker who can submit repeated webhooks recover a valid signature byte by byte. Use the same primitive as the adjacent helper: `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. (Note `compare_digest` raises TypeError on non-str/bytes input, so if `header` can be `None` from an absent HTTP header, guard with `if header is None: return False` first.)

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook HMAC compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: Public API contract undocumented: verify_acmepay uses unsafe comparison
findings.body: The function `verify_acmepay` is a public API (parallels `verify_stripe`) but has no docstring. More critically, its implementation uses `==` for comparison (line 12) whereas the parallel `verify_stripe` function uses `hmac.compare_digest` (line 7). A caller cannot infer from the name or signature that one is timing-safe and one is not. The existing function's safety property is now part of an implicit, undocumented contract that this new function violates in the same module, making it likely a caller would use both and believe both safe.

findings.title: No test covers verify_acmepay's signature comparison behaviour
findings.body: verify_acmepay is new logic with a distinct return path (expected == header) from verify_stripe's compare_digest-based check, but no test file is included in this diff. Nothing would catch a change to this comparison's behavior (e.g. accidentally always returning True/False, or a typo in the field being compared) since there is no assertion anywhere exercising verify_acmepay with valid/invalid signatures.

findings.title: Stack trace and exception text returned to the client on 500
findings.body:
`handle(exc)` previously returned a fixed `"internal error"` string; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP 500 response body. Any unauthenticated caller who can provoke an unhandled exception (malformed input, oversized payload, a poisoned parameter) receives absolute source file paths, module and function names, line numbers, the framework/ORM stack, and whatever the exception message happens to contain — DB error text with table/column names and fragments of the failing SQL, connection strings in `OperationalError` messages, key material or tokens embedded in exception arguments from HTTP client libraries. That is a free map of the application's internals for anyone probing it, and it makes finding the next bug substantially cheaper.

The stated goal — on-call sees what failed without SSHing in — is already met by the `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8, which captures the same traceback server-side. Keep the response opaque and give operators a correlation handle instead:

```python
def handle(exc):
    incident_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"incident_id": incident_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "incident_id": incident_id}, 500
```

If verbose bodies are genuinely wanted for a local dev loop, gate them behind an explicit debug flag that is off by default in production config rather than emitting them unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() may not correspond to the passed exc

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape and value changed for existing callers

findings.title: No test verifies the new error response shape/content
findings.body: The `handle` function's return value changed from a generic error message to one embedding the raw exception string and full traceback. There is no test in this diff exercising `handle()` and asserting on the returned dict's contents. If this behavior is reverted, weakened, or accidentally broadened further (e.g., leaking more internal detail), nothing would fail. Given this is also a sensitive change (exposing internals in API responses), a test that calls `handle(exc)` and asserts the shape/content of the returned tuple would catch regressions in either direction.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password hash with a single unsalted MD5 round, while `hash_password` two lines above uses bcrypt with a per-password salt. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash: an attacker who obtains the stored values (dump, backup, log leak) can recover the plaintexts at billions of guesses per second, and the lack of a salt makes rainbow-table and cross-user duplicate detection trivial. If these values are also compared against a user-supplied reset token or password, the weak hash becomes the authentication check itself.

Use the same primitive as the main path: `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`, and verify with `bcrypt.checkpw` (constant-time) rather than string equality. If the intent was to hash a *reset token* rather than a password, use `hashlib.sha256` at minimum and compare with `hmac.compare_digest`, and name the function accordingly.

findings.title: Reset password hash format incompatible with existing bcrypt hashes
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while the new `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest. If both write into the same stored-password field, the verification path (presumably `bcrypt.checkpw`) cannot validate an MD5 digest: `bcrypt.checkpw` raises `ValueError` on an invalid salt/hash rather than returning `False`, so a user who completes a reset will hit an error or be permanently locked out. Either route reset passwords through `hash_password` so the stored format stays uniform, or make the verification side explicitly format-aware. findings.title: pull_request_target + fork head checkout runs untrusted code with secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with the repository's default (typically write) permissions, and it is triggered by pull requests from forks with no approval gate. Line 12 then checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — code the pull request author fully controls, including `scripts/measure.sh` itself — and line 13 executes it with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected on lines 14-15.

Entry point: an attacker opens a PR from a fork containing a modified `scripts/measure.sh` (or any file it sources, or a `package.json` lifecycle hook / dependency it installs). Sink: `- run: ./scripts/measure.sh` on line 13, executed on a runner that holds `NPM_TOKEN` in its environment and a privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN` in the credential helper configured by `actions/checkout`. The attacker exfiltrates the npm publish token and can push to the repository or tamper with the checkout credentials.

Fixes, in order of preference:
- Revert to `pull_request`. Fork PRs still get the size-check CI signal; they just run without secrets. If `measure.sh` genuinely needs `NPM_TOKEN` (e.g. a private registry), split it: run the untrusted build under `pull_request` with no secrets, and do any privileged step in a separate `workflow_run`/`pull_request_target` job that does **not** check out fork code.
- If `pull_request_target` must stay, do not check out the head SHA, do not run any script from the PR ref, add `permissions: contents: read`, and set `persist-credentials: false` on the checkout.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target + untrusted checkout runs fork code with secrets

findings.title: Digest key requires JSON-serializable context; old key only required hashable
findings.body:
The previous key `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` accepted any *hashable* value — `datetime`, `Decimal`, `UUID`, enums, frozen dataclasses, arbitrary objects. `json.dumps` accepts only JSON types and raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those. Any existing caller that passes such a value in `context` now gets an exception from the cache layer instead of a render, and the failure happens before `_render` is ever called, so it is not something the template engine can absorb.

If the digest approach is kept, pass a `default=repr` (or a custom encoder) to `json.dumps` so unknown types degrade to a stable string instead of raising, and be explicit that `repr`-based keys can alias. Note `sort_keys=True` also raises `TypeError` for a context with mixed-type keys (e.g. `{1: ..., "a": ...}`), which the old tuple key handled via `sorted` only when types were comparable — same class of regression.

The new key serializes context with `json.dumps`, which normalizes tuples to lists and coerces non-string dict keys to strings. Two contexts that were previously distinct cache keys can now collide and silently return a stale cached render. None of the added tests (`test_key_is_by_value_not_by_identity`, `test_different_context_renders_again`) exercise this, since they only use plain int values with string keys.

findings.title: Rate limit bypassable: unsynchronised check-then-act in try_consume
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 — all outside `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` (line 9) correctly holds for the same state.

Two consequences, both attacker-reachable by simply issuing requests concurrently (the normal mode of an async server):

1. **Limit bypass.** N coroutines can each pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check on line 16 before any of them writes, so N*cost is admitted against a budget of `cost`. The amount over the limit scales with the attacker's concurrency.
2. **Lost updates make the bypass permanent.** Line 19 assigns an absolute value computed from a stale read rather than incrementing, so concurrent calls clobber each other's accounting. The stored counter drifts permanently below actual consumption, meaning the limiter never catches up even after the burst ends.

Fix: hold the lock across the read, the decision and the write, and drop the `await` from the critical section (or use an atomic increment-then-rollback):

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ try_consume checks and writes across an await without holding _lock

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Counters never decay, so LIMIT is a lifetime cap not a rate limit

Under concurrent calls for the same tenant, two coroutines can both read the same 'current' value, both pass the limit check, and both write, allowing the tenant to exceed LIMIT — exactly the race the rate limiter is meant to prevent. findings.title: File handle leaked on header-mismatch return and on exceptions

findings.title: Retry around non-idempotent charge can double-charge customers
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge. Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure after the gateway has already accepted the request (timeout, dropped connection, 5xx on the response leg) causes a second and possibly third charge to be created. The customer is billed 2–3x with no way for the caller to detect it.

The gateway docstring states it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a stable key per logical charge attempt (e.g. derived from an order/payment id, not per-retry) and pass it through `charge()` so the gateway collapses retries into one charge. Only then is the retry decorator safe here. Alternatively, drop the retry on this path and reconcile via `get_charge`.

The retry on `fetch_charge` (line 5–7) is fine: `get_charge` is a documented-safe GET.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge without an Idempotency-Key

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ charge_card retries non-idempotent call without Idempotency-Key

findings.title: No test guards against duplicate charges from retrying a non-idempotent call

If a transient failure occurs after the gateway processed the charge (e.g., timeout on the response), the retry will create a second charge. Nothing in this diff exercises charge_card under a simulated flaky-then-success scenario to check that only one charge is created; a test asserting on retry.call_count or on the mocked charge() call count would not catch this since it would just confirm the function was called 3 times, not that duplicate real-world charges resulted.

findings.title: Naive/aware datetime subtraction raises TypeError in expires_within
findings.body: `datetime.now()` returns a naive local datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just edge cases. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. As a secondary point, even with the timezone fixed the local-vs-UTC mismatch would silently shift the cutoff by the machine's UTC offset.

findings.title: Public function violates documented timezone-aware contract
findings.body: The new `expires_within` function computes `cutoff = datetime.now().replace(microsecond=0)` on line 9, which produces a timezone-naive datetime. The function's contract—what a caller should reasonably expect it to do—is now inconsistent with the established invariant. A caller who relies on the documented behaviour that `expires_at` is timezone-aware UTC cannot safely use this function, as comparing timezone-aware and timezone-naive datetimes in Python raises TypeError. Either use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` (as the existing `is_expired` does on line 5) or document why this function deliberately breaks the timezone-aware invariant.

findings.title: expires_within also returns True for already-expired invites

If callers use this to drive reminder emails or warnings, already-dead invites will be included. If that is not intended, guard with `0 <= delta.total_seconds() < hours * 3600` or compose with `not is_expired(invite)`.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it directly, so for any account that has not completed onboarding this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. findings.title: Timeout units mismatch with fetch() contract
findings.body: The call to `fetch()` passes `timeout=30`, but according to the `fetch()` docstring in `clients/http.py`, the timeout parameter expects MILLISECONDS. This means the actual timeout will be 30ms, not 30 seconds as intended by the PR description ('Timeout set generously'). Either convert to milliseconds (30000) or update the `fetch()` call to match its documented contract.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds

Passing `timeout=30` gives the partner API 30ms to respond, which contradicts the PR's stated intent of a generous timeout for a slow API. The call will likely fail every night — and because the default `retries=3` shares the same budget, the retries will not help. findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue() has no test covering its fetch call/timeout
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() is added with no accompanying test. It calls fetch(url, timeout=30), but clients/http.py documents timeout as being in MILLISECONDS. findings.title: Duplicate index: invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC) already exists
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` has exactly the same definition as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in migration 0007 — same table, same column list, same `created_at DESC` ordering. `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on the index *name* only, so it will not suppress this; Postgres will happily build a second, fully redundant copy. Drop this statement, or if the intent is to replace the old index, drop `invoices_tenant_created_idx` explicitly.

findings.title: Referer logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token into logs
findings.body:
Line 5 now writes `request.headers[header]` directly for every header, including `Referer`. The previous code routed Referer through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` precisely because notebook URLs are handed out as `?token=...` (see `token_authenticated_url` in `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`), so the browser attaches the live auth token in the Referer of every subresource request. Any 5xx now serialises that token into the log stream, where it is readable by anyone with log access and typically survives log shipping/retention — a full session credential.

Restore the conditional scrub for `Referer` (and keep passing `extra_param_keys` through) rather than logging the raw value. As a secondary consequence, `extra_param_keys` appears to be left unused by this function now, which is a signal the sanitisation path was dropped wholesale rather than intentionally replaced.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaked into logs via unscrubbed Referer header

findings.title: Removed Referer scrubbing has no regression test
findings.body: The change deletes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, which per identity.py exists specifically because Referer can carry the auth token from token_authenticated_url. There is no test in this diff verifying that logged headers redact the token, so a future revert or similar refactor removing scrubbing would go undetected.

findings.title: xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, re-enabling SVG XSS
findings.body: `validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` falls out of that branch and is no longer scheme-validated, so markup such as `` in user-submitted markdown reaches the DOM with an executable URL. In browsers that still honour `xlink:href` this is stored XSS against every viewer of the content. If the intent was genuinely to stop supporting the attribute, it must be removed from whatever attribute allowlist permits it to be emitted (or explicitly rejected here with `return false`) rather than merely dropped from the scheme check — dropping it from the check only removes the guard while the attribute keeps rendering. Suggested fix: restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` on line 6, or add an explicit deny for it. _Also raised by the correctness agent:_ xlinkhref no longer validated against unsafe URL schemes

findings.title: No visible test covers xlinkhref no longer being sanitised
findings.body: The change removes the 'xlinkhref' check from validateProp's dangerous-link guard, meaning any 'xlinkhref' attribute now falls through to whatever default handling exists (likely allowed unconditionally) instead of being checked via isAnchorLinkAllowed. Since this attribute previously received the same unsafe-link screening as href/src, this is a security-relevant behavior change. No test file is included in this diff, and no existing test evidence was provided showing xlinkhref sanitisation is exercised elsewhere. If validateProp is not covered by a test asserting that a 'javascript:'-prefixed xlinkhref value is rejected, this regression (or any future reintroduction of the vulnerability) would go undetected.

findings.title: Unvalidated project query param reaches buildPath, enabling path traversal
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, is no longer checked by `common.ValidateID` before it flows on to the file DAO. The retrieved `buildPath` explicitly states: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." This hunk removes exactly that caller-side validation.

The justification that "the path join already scopes under the folder root" does not hold: `filepath.Join` applies `Clean`, which *resolves* `..` segments rather than rejecting them, so `filepath.Join("/data", "../../etc", kind)` yields `/etc/<kind>` — outside the storage root. A value such as `?project=../../..%2Fsomething` therefore escapes the folder root, and even without traversal an unconstrained name can be used to address documents the ID grammar was meant to exclude.

Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check (returning `HandleBadRequestError`) before the parameter is used, or push an equivalent validation into `buildPath` itself so the contract is enforced in one place.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing ValidateID lets project query param traverse out of storage root

findings.title: buildPath caller no longer validates project name
findings.body: The buildPath function's documentation (in file.go) states that callers are required to validate names before calling it. This diff removes the ValidateID check on projectQueryParameter, breaking that contract. The list() function now passes an unvalidated projectQueryParameter to buildPath without performing the validation the API contract requires.

findings.title: No test covers that invalid project query params are now accepted
findings.body: The removed validation call previously rejected malformed/malicious projectQueryParameter values (e.g. path traversal sequences like '../') before they could reach buildPath, which per its own documented contract performs no validation itself and relies on callers to have validated names. This diff removes that check but adds no test asserting the new behavior (that such values are now passed through) nor any test verifying downstream handling is still safe. If this change is wrong — e.g. it reintroduces a path traversal vulnerability — nothing in the existing or added test suite would fail, since there is no test exercising list() with an invalid project name.

findings.title: Buffer reserved from attacker-declared Content-Length before reading body
findings.body:
`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` sizes the buffer from `contentLength`, which for an S3 `UploadPart` request originates in the client-supplied `Content-Length` header (the parameter is passed in from the HTTP handler, see signature on line 2). Nothing in this function verifies that the declared length matches the bytes actually delivered, or that it is within any per-part limit — the `io.Copy` on line 8 only discovers the true size afterwards.

Consequences:

- A client can send `Content-Length: 5368709120` with a one-byte body and make the server commit gigabytes of heap per in-flight request. Repeating this across concurrent connections is a cheap remote OOM / denial of service; the attacker pays almost no bandwidth.
- If `contentLength` can be `-1` or `0` (chunked / unknown-length transfer encoding, which the previous growth-on-demand code handled naturally), `Reserve` is being called with a value it may not expect; depending on its implementation that is a panic or a silently wrong capacity.

Suggested fix: clamp before reserving, e.g. only reserve when `contentLength > 0`, cap it at the configured maximum part size (`min(contentLength, maxPartSize)`), and reject or fall back to incremental growth otherwise. Pair that with enforcing the declared length against the bytes actually copied so an over-declared part is rejected rather than silently accepted.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from attacker-declared Content-Length

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Reserve(contentLength) unguarded for unknown/negative length

findings.title: No test covers pre-reservation against actual body size
findings.body: The change now pre-allocates the multipart buffer using the caller-supplied contentLength via Reserve(contentLength). There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises the case where contentLength does not match the actual bytes read from body (e.g., a Content-Length larger or smaller than the real upload, or a very large declared length). If Reserve's behavior changes, or if it causes incorrect allocation/growth handling relative to the actual number of bytes copied, nothing would catch it — the existing io.Copy path just proceeds and returns n, err, and no assertion in the visible code path checks that pre-reservation had any effect or that mismatched lengths are handled safely.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The previous expression (`"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`) was a deliberate fail-secure default: TLS was used unless the caller explicitly opted out with `is_secure=False`. The new ternary treats every falsy value — including the common case where `is_secure` is simply absent from `request.meta` and `.get()` returns `None` — as a request for plaintext. Since `is_secure` is opt-in metadata that most callers never set, the effective default for all S3 downloads flips from HTTPS to HTTP.

The resulting URL on line 6 is the transport for requests that carry AWS authorization material (signature/date headers, and for the legacy v2 scheme an `AWSAccessKeyId`/`Signature` pair that can appear in the query string preserved on line 5). Anyone on the network path can read the object contents and replay or reuse the signed request.

Restore the fail-secure form, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, so that only an explicit `False` downgrades the connection.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Default S3 scheme flips from https to http when is_secure is unset

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ S3 scheme logic inverted: defaults now insecure

findings.title: Scheme-default change has no accompanying test
findings.body: The old logic defaulted to https unless is_secure was explicitly False; the new logic defaults to http unless is_secure is truthy. This changes behavior for the common case where is_secure is absent from request.meta (e.g. None or missing), switching the resulting URL from https to http. No test file is included in this diff, so if this default flip is unintended (a security-relevant regression), nothing would fail to signal it.

findings.title: DELETE now maps to "push", granting delete to push-only accounts
findings.body:
The removed `switch` mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the distinct action `"delete"`. The new condition only special-cases GET and HEAD, so DELETE falls into the `!= GET && != HEAD` branch and requests `"push"`.

Two consequences, both authorization failures:

1. Any account authorized for `push` on a repository can now delete tags/manifests, because the access check it is measured against is the push grant. The retrieved config comment states the separation is deliberate: "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones."
2. `ResourceAction.Action` is never `"delete"` any more, so existing policies that grant only `delete` no longer match anything and those accounts lose the ability they were configured for.

Keep the DELETE case explicit:

```go
action := "pull"
switch request.Method {
case http.MethodGet, http.MethodHead:
    action = "pull"
case http.MethodDelete:
    action = "delete"
default:
    action = "push"
}
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorised as "push"; delete permission check removed

findings.title: Action mapping no longer matches documented contract
findings.body: The code change collapses the three-action model (pull, push, delete) documented in pkg/api/config/config.go into a two-action model (pull, push). The DELETE HTTP method is no longer mapped to ActionDelete, but instead to ActionPush. The repository documentation explicitly states that 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' This change breaks that contract without updating the documentation, making callers who rely on the documented behavior incorrect.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE now mapping to push instead of delete
findings.body: The change collapses the previous three-way method-to-action mapping (pull/push/delete) into a two-way one, so HTTP DELETE requests now resolve to action "push" instead of "delete". Per the repo's own documented access model (pkg/api/config/config.go), pull/push/delete are intentionally distinct so an account can push without being able to delete. This diff contains no test changes, so if this mapping is wrong (e.g. it should have stayed "delete", or the collapse is an unintended regression), nothing in the test suite would fail. A test asserting that DELETE requests map to a specific action is needed to catch regressions here.

findings.title: Function name `get_tenant_fresh` is misleading about side effects
findings.body:
The function name `get_tenant_fresh` follows the `get_*` convention, which typically implies a read-only operation. However, this function has significant side effects: it modifies the shared `_CACHE` dictionary and clears it when it exceeds 1000 entries. A caller familiar with `get_tenant()` would reasonably expect `get_tenant_fresh()` to be a variant that bypasses the cache, not one that mutates it. The name should either (1) be changed to reflect that it mutates the cache (e.g., `fetch_and_cache_tenant`), or (2) the function should be documented with a docstring explaining the cache side effects. Without this, callers risk misusing the function or introducing unexpected cache clears.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Size guard clears the whole shared cache, discarding the fresh entry

findings.title: New get_tenant_fresh function has no test coverage
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces new behavior: it fetches fresh data, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. If the cache-write were wrong (e.g. wrong key, stale tenant object) or the eviction threshold/logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, clearing too aggressively, or never clearing causing unbounded growth), nothing would fail — the function would simply return whatever _fetch returns, masking the side-effect bugs.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id keys shared cache; 1000-entry clear flushes all tenants
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` uses `tenant_id` directly as the key of the module-level `_CACHE` (line 10) with no validation that the id is well-formed or that the caller may act on that tenant, and the eviction policy on lines 11-12 is a full `clear()` of the shared dict. If any request-facing caller passes a client-supplied id here, a caller can (a) insert an unbounded number of distinct keys, each holding whatever `_fetch` returns, and (b) by exceeding 1000 entries, evict every other tenant's cached entry at will, turning a cheap loop into repeated backing-store load for all tenants. Consider a bounded LRU (e.g. `functools.lru_cache` or an explicit LRU with per-key eviction instead of `clear()`), and validate/normalise `tenant_id` before it becomes a key. Note also that a `None` result from `_fetch` is cached, so a failed lookup for an unknown id persists as a negative entry that `get_tenant` cannot distinguish from a miss.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts new return type

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail to import
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, but this is an absolute import. Every other import in this file is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`).
